Introduction

Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is myocardial necrosis due to prolonged ischaemia, usually from coronary artery thrombosis over an atherosclerotic plaque. ST-elevation MI (STEMI) requires immediate reperfusion; non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI) requires antithrombotic therapy and risk-stratified invasive strategy. Goal — restore coronary patency, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, prevent complications, improve survival.

Phases of Treatment

  1. Pre-hospital — aspirin 300 mg chewed; nitroglycerin sublingual if BP allows; oxygen if hypoxic; morphine for pain; immediate transfer to PCI-capable hospital.
  2. Immediate (reperfusion) — primary PCI (preferred) or fibrinolysis (if PCI not available within 120 min).
  3. Antiplatelet & anticoagulant therapy.
  4. Adjunctive therapy — β-blocker, ACEI/ARB, statin.
  5. Secondary prevention & long-term.

Pharmacotherapy

1. Reperfusion Therapy

  • Primary PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention):
    • Preferred if performed within 90 min of first medical contact (door-to-balloon time).
    • Stenting (drug-eluting stent preferred); aspiration thrombectomy; GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor (abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban) during PCI.
  • Fibrinolytic therapy (thrombolysis):
    • If PCI unavailable within 120 min; door-to-needle time <30 min.
    • Streptokinase — 1.5 million U IV over 60 min (historical; cheapest; antigenic — single use; allergic reactions; hypotension).
    • Alteplase (rt-PA) — 15 mg IV bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 min (max 50 mg), then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 min (max 35 mg); total max 100 mg.
    • Reteplase (r-PA) — 10 U IV over 2 min × 2 doses, 30 min apart.
    • Tenecteplase (TNK-t-PA) — single bolus 0.5 mg/kg (max 50 mg); preferred — easy, weight-based, fewer non-cerebral bleeds.
    • Contraindications — active bleeding, recent stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, intracranial neoplasm, severe hypertension (>180/110), recent surgery, aortic dissection, pregnancy.

2. Antiplatelet Therapy

  • Aspirin:
    • Loading dose — 300 mg chewed (non-enteric-coated) ASAP; then 75–100 mg daily lifelong.
    • Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 in platelets → ↓ thromboxane A2 → ↓ platelet aggregation.
    • Reduces mortality by ~25% in AMI.
  • P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonists:
    • Ticagrelor — 180 mg loading then 90 mg BD; reversible; faster onset; preferred with aspirin (PLATO trial — reduced mortality vs clopidogrel); contraindicated in history of intracranial haemorrhage; dyspnoea side effect.
    • Prasugrel — 60 mg loading then 10 mg daily; irreversible; more potent than clopidogrel; avoid in age >75, weight <60 kg, history of stroke/TIA (bleeding risk); used in PCI.
    • Clopidogrel — 600 mg loading (PCI) or 300 mg (fibrinolysis) then 75 mg daily; irreversible; prodrug (CYP2C19) — variable response; genetic polymorphism; cheapest.
    • Duration — DAPT (dual antiplatelet therapy) for 12 months post-STEMI (with drug-eluting stent); then aspirin lifelong; ticagrelor 60 mg BD monotherapy or with aspirin beyond 1 year in high-risk (PEGASUS trial).
  • GP IIb/IIIa antagonists — abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban; during PCI for thrombus burden; less used with newer P2Y12 inhibitors.

3. Anticoagulant Therapy

  • Unfractionated heparin (UFH) — 60 IU/kg bolus (max 4000 IU), then 12 IU/kg/h infusion (target aPTT 1.5–2× control); used during PCI & with fibrinolytics (alteplase, reteplase, tenecteplase).
  • Enoxaparin (LMWH) — 1 mg/kg SC every 12 h; preferred with fibrinolytics in patients <75 yr (for >75 yr — 0.75 mg/kg every 12 h; renal adjustment if CrCl <30); ExTRACT-TIMI 25 trial.
  • Fondaparinux — 2.5 mg IV then SC daily; preferred in conservative strategy (OASIS-6 trial); not for PCI (catheter thrombosis risk).
  • Bivalirudin — direct thrombin inhibitor; used in primary PCI (reduces bleeding vs heparin + GP IIb/IIIa; HORIZONS-AMI trial).
  • Duration — until hospital discharge or PCI completion; longer if LV thrombus, AF, mechanical valve.

4. Adjunctive Anti-ischaemic & Cardioprotective Therapy

  • β-Blockers:
    • Started within 24 h if no contraindication (heart failure, hypotension, bradycardia, AV block, severe asthma).
    • Metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol; oral.
    • IV esmolol if tachyarrhythmia, hypertension, ongoing ischaemia.
    • Reduces mortality, reinfarction, arrhythmias; long-term for secondary prevention.
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs:
    • Started within 24 h if no contraindication (hypotension, bilateral renal artery stenosis, pregnancy, hyperkalaemia, angioedema history).
    • Especially beneficial in anterior MI, LV dysfunction (EF <40%), heart failure, diabetes, hypertension.
    • Ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril, perindopril; valsartan, losartan, telmisartan if ACEI intolerant.
    • Reduces mortality, remodelling, heart failure.
    • ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) in post-MI HFrEF (PARADISE-MI trial — emerging).
  • Statins:
    • High-intensity — atorvastatin 80 mg daily or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg daily; started within 24 h; continued lifelong.
    • Target LDL <70 mg/dL (or <55 mg/dL in very high-risk per ESC 2019).
    • Plaque stabilisation; anti-inflammatory; ↓ mortality.
    • Add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab, alirocumab) if target not met.
  • Nitrates:
    • Sublingual GTN for ongoing chest pain; IV nitroglycerin for persistent pain, hypertension, acute LV failure.
    • Avoid in hypotension (SBP <90), RV infarction, recent PDE5 inhibitor.
    • No mortality benefit; symptom relief.
  • Morphine:
    • 5–10 mg IV for pain, anxiety, pulmonary oedema; reduces sympathetic drive & preload.
    • Caution — may delay antiplatelet absorption (↓ ticagrelor/clopidogrel levels); use judiciously.
  • Oxygen — only if SpO₂ <90% or respiratory distress; routine O₂ may worsen outcome in normoxic patients (AVOID trial).
  • Electrolytes — maintain K⁺ >4.0, Mg²⁺ >2.0; reduce arrhythmias.

5. Secondary Prevention (Lifelong)

  • Aspirin (lifelong) + P2Y12 inhibitor (12 months — longer if high thrombotic risk).
  • β-blocker (lifelong — especially if LV dysfunction).
  • ACEI/ARB (lifelong — especially if LV dysfunction, diabetes, hypertension).
  • High-intensity statin (lifelong); target LDL <70 mg/dL.
  • Aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone 25–50 mg daily) if LV EF ≤40% & heart failure or diabetes (EPHESUS trial).
  • Lifestyle — smoking cessation; Mediterranean diet; exercise; cardiac rehabilitation; weight management; diabetes control; BP control.
  • Vaccination — annual influenza; pneumococcal.
  • Treat comorbidities — hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, OSA.

Complications & Their Treatment

  • Arrhythmias — VT/VF (defibrillation; amiodarone; lidocaine); AF (anticoagulate; rate control with β-blocker; cardiovert if unstable); bradycardia/AV block (atropine; temporary pacemaker).
  • Acute heart failure — IV furosemide; nitrates; oxygen; NIV; inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) if hypotensive; mechanical support (IABP, Impella, ECMO).
  • Cardiogenic shock — early revascularisation; inotropes; vasopressors; mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, ECMO).
  • Mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture) — surgical repair.
  • LV thrombus — anticoagulation (warfarin or DOAC) 3–6 months.
  • Pericarditis (Dressler) — aspirin high dose; NSAIDs; corticosteroids if refractory.

Clinical Pearl

Time is muscle — every minute of delay in reperfusion results in additional myocardial necrosis; door-to-balloon time <90 min for primary PCI; door-to-needle time <30 min for fibrinolysis. Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor preferred) + anticoagulant (heparin/enoxaparin/bivalirudin) + statin + β-blocker + ACEI form the pharmacological backbone of AMI management. Ticagrelor + aspirin is preferred DAPT in STEMI/NSTEMI (PLATO trial — reduced all-cause mortality vs clopidogrel); but higher dyspnoea, bleeding risk. Prasugrel — more potent; avoid in age >75, weight <60 kg, history of stroke/TIA. Primary PCI is superior to fibrinolysis if performed within 90 min; fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable within 120 min; tenecteplase single bolus preferred (easiest). Always check contraindications to fibrinolysis — active bleeding, recent stroke, intracranial surgery/neoplasm, severe hypertension, aortic dissection. High-intensity statin within 24 h — atorvastatin 80 mg daily; target LDL <70 mg/dL; add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor if not achieved. β-blocker within 24 h if no contraindication — reduces mortality; avoid in acute heart failure, hypotension, bradycardia, severe asthma. ACEI within 24 h — especially anterior MI, LV dysfunction, diabetes; reduces remodelling & mortality. Eplerenone — if LV EF ≤40% + heart failure or diabetes (EPHESUS trial). Cardiac rehabilitation — exercise, education, psychological support, secondary prevention; reduces mortality by 20–30%. India — STEMI mortality high; access to PCI limited in rural areas; fibrinolysis (streptokinase — cheap) still widely used; AMI registry & systems of care (hub-and-spoke model) improving outcomes.

Introduction

Drug antagonism is the phenomenon where the combined effect of two drugs is less than the sum of their individual effects (i.e., one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another). It is the opposite of synergism (potentiation/additive). Antagonism is exploited therapeutically (antidotes, treatment of overdose) and is also an important source of adverse drug interactions.

Types of Drug Antagonism

1. Pharmaceutical Antagonism (Incompatibility)

  • Definition — two drugs react chemically or physically before administration or in the body, resulting in inactivation or precipitation.
  • Mechanism:
    • Chemical reaction — acid + base neutralisation; chelation; oxidation-reduction.
    • Physical — precipitation; adsorption; pH changes.
  • Examples:
    • Protamine sulphate + heparin — positively charged protamine binds negatively charged heparin → neutralises anticoagulant effect (used as heparin antidote).
    • Chelating agents + heavy metals — EDTA, dimercaprol (BAL), penicillamine, succimer (DMSA), deferoxamine bind & remove lead, mercury, arsenic, iron.
    • Activated charcoal + drugs — adsorbs drugs in gut; prevents absorption (used in poisoning).
    • Tetracyclines + calcium/magnesium/iron/aluminium antacids or dairy — chelation; ↓ tetracycline absorption.
    • Fluoroquinolones + antacids — chelation; ↓ absorption.
    • Penicillin + aminoglycosides (in same IV line) — penicillin binds aminoglycosides → inactivation.
    • Phenytoin + dextrose infusion — phenytoin precipitates in dextrose; give in normal saline.
    • Sulphadiazine silver + enzymes — inactivation.

2. Pharmacokinetic Antagonism

One drug reduces the effective concentration of another at the site of action by altering its absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion.

  • Absorption:
    • Antacids (pH change) ↓ ketoconazole, itraconazole, atazanavir absorption.
    • Cholestyramine, colestipol bind bile acids & drugs (warfarin, thyroxine, digoxin) in gut.
    • Activated charcoal (poisoning).
    • Metoclopramide speeds gastric emptying (↑ rate but variable extent); anticholinergics slow it.
    • Iron + tea (tannins) — ↓ absorption.
  • Distribution:
    • Displacement from plasma protein binding — warfarin displaced by NSAIDs, sulfonamides, chloral hydrate → transient ↑ free warfarin → ↑ anticoagulation.
    • Usually clinically significant only for highly bound drugs with narrow therapeutic index.
  • Metabolism (most important clinically):
    • Enzyme induction — rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, griseofulvin, St John's wort, alcohol (chronic), smoking → ↑ CYP450 → ↓ effect of warfarin, OCPs, theophylline, cyclosporine, HIV protease inhibitors, corticosteroids.
    • Enzyme inhibition — macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), azole antifungals (ketoconazole, fluconazole, itraconazole), cimetidine, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), amiodarone, diltiazem, verapamil, grapefruit juice, SSRIs (fluoxetine, fluvoxamine), metronidazole, sulfonamides, protease inhibitors → ↓ metabolism → ↑ effect of warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin, carbamazepine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin), benzodiazepines.
  • Excretion:
    • Altered renal tubular secretion — probenecid inhibits OAT (organic anion transporter) → ↓ penicillin excretion → ↑ penicillin levels (historical use — syphilis, gonorrhoea); also ↓ excretion of methotrexate, NSAIDs, furosemide.
    • Urinary pH alteration — sodium bicarbonate alkalinises urine → ↑ excretion of weak acids (salicylates, phenobarbital); ammonium chloride acidifies urine → ↑ excretion of weak bases (amphetamine, phencyclidine).
    • Lithium + NSAIDs/thiazides — ↓ lithium excretion → toxicity.
    • Digoxin + verapamil/quinidine/amiodarone — ↓ digoxin clearance (P-gp inhibition) → toxicity.

3. Pharmacodynamic Antagonism

Both drugs act at the same or different receptors/physiological systems but produce opposite physiological effects.

  • Competitive (surmountable) antagonism:
    • Antagonist binds reversibly to the same receptor as agonist; can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (rightward shift of dose-response curve, no change in Emax).
    • Examples:
      • Acetylcholine (muscarinic) vs atropine — atropine is competitive muscarinic antagonist (organophosphorus poisoning antidote).
      • Histamine (H1) vs antihistamines — cetirizine, fexofenadine, chlorpheniramine.
      • Adrenaline (β) vs propranolol — β-blocker.
      • Morphine (μ) vs naloxone — opioid antagonist (opioid overdose).
      • Angiotensin II (AT1) vs losartan — ARB.
      • Benzodiazepine vs flumazenil — antidote.
      • Suxamethonium vs neostigmine — neuromuscular blockade reversal.
      • Salbutamol (β2) vs propranolol — propranolol blocks bronchodilator effect → bronchospasm in asthmatics.
  • Non-competitive (insurmountable) antagonism:
    • Antagonist binds irreversibly (covalent bond) or to a different (allosteric) site; cannot be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (↓ Emax, may or may not shift curve rightward).
    • Examples:
      • Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible α-blocker) vs adrenaline — phaeochromocytoma preparation.
      • Aspirin (irreversible COX inhibitor) vs thromboxane — antiplatelet effect lasts 7–10 days (platelet lifespan).
      • Omeprazole (irreversible H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibitor) vs gastric acid.
      • MAO inhibitors vs tyramine — cheese reaction.
      • Sulfonylureas vs diazoxide — insulin vs hyperglycaemia.
      • Ketamine (NMDA channel blocker) — use-dependent non-competitive.
  • Physiological (functional) antagonism:
    • Two drugs act at different receptors or systems to produce opposite physiological effects; cancels out.
    • Examples:
      • Histamine vs adrenaline — histamine lowers BP (vasodilation); adrenaline raises BP (vasoconstriction); adrenaline used in anaphylaxis (physiological antagonist of histamine).
      • Insulin vs glucagon/catecholamines/glucocorticoids — insulin lowers blood glucose; others raise it.
      • Acetylcholine (muscarinic) vs adrenaline (β1) — ACh slows heart; adrenaline speeds it.
      • Glucagon vs propranolol — glucagon increases heart rate via different receptor; used in β-blocker overdose.
      • Levodopa vs antipsychotics — dopamine vs dopamine antagonism; worsen Parkinson's.
  • Chemical antagonism:
    • One drug binds directly to another (not receptor) & inactivates it.
    • Examples:
      • Protamine + heparin — neutralisation (also pharmaceutical).
      • Dimercaprol (BAL) + heavy metals — chelation.
      • Deferoxamine + iron — chelation.
      • Digoxin-specific Fab antibody (DigiFab) + digoxin — binds and removes digoxin.
      • Idarucizumab + dabigatran — monoclonal antibody binds dabigatran.
      • Andexanet alfa + rivaroxaban/apixaban — decoy factor Xa.
  • Allosteric antagonism:
    • Antagonist binds to a different site on the receptor, causing conformational change that reduces agonist affinity or efficacy.
    • Examples:
      • Picrotoxin vs GABA-A — blocks chloride channel (different site from GABA).
      • Naloxone at very high doses — may have allosteric effects.

Quantitative Aspects — Dose-Response Curves

  • Competitive antagonist — produces parallel rightward shift of agonist dose-response curve; Emax unchanged; can be overcome by ↑ agonist dose.
  • Non-competitive antagonist — ↓ Emax (maximum response reduced); may or may not shift curve; cannot be overcome by ↑ agonist dose.
  • pA₂ — negative logarithm of the molar concentration of antagonist that requires doubling of agonist concentration to produce the same response as before; measure of antagonist potency (Schild plot).

Clinical Significance

  • Therapeutic uses — antidotes (naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines, atropine + pralidoxime for organophosphates, protamine for heparin, vitamin K for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, digoxin Fab for digoxin); treatment of overdose (charcoal for many poisons); reversing adverse effects.
  • Adverse drug interactions — reduce therapeutic effect of essential drugs (warfarin + rifampin → ↓ anticoagulation → thrombosis; OCPs + rifampin → contraceptive failure; theophylline + phenytoin → ↓ theophylline → asthma exacerbation).
  • Contraindications — β-blockers in asthma (block β2 bronchodilator effect of adrenaline); prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors in pregnancy (maintain ductus arteriosus patency — indomethacin closes PDA).
  • Combination therapy — sometimes desired (antihypertensive combination — ACEI + thiazide, ACEI + CCB; antibiotics — β-lactam + aminoglycoside synergy).

Clinical Pearl

Distinguish competitive from non-competitive antagonism by dose-response curve — competitive produces parallel rightward shift (Emax unchanged, overcome by ↑ agonist); non-competitive reduces Emax (cannot be overcome). Aspirin is a non-competitive irreversible COX inhibitor — antiplatelet effect lasts 7–10 days (platelet lifespan); must stop 7 days before surgery. Phenoxybenzamine is the only irreversible α-blocker — used pre-operatively for phaeochromocytoma; effect lasts days until new α-receptors synthesised. Always check for pharmacokinetic interactions when adding or stopping drugs — rifampin (potent enzyme inducer) reduces warfarin, OCP, tacrolimus, HIV PIs, levothyroxine; macrolides + statins ↑ rhabdomyolysis risk; grapefruit juice ↑ statin, CCB, cyclosporine levels (intestinal CYP3A4 inhibition). Naloxone is the prototypical competitive antagonist — opioid overdose; titrate to respiratory rate, not full consciousness (avoid withdrawal); short half-life (1 h) — may need infusion for long-acting opioids (methadone, fentanyl, tramadol). Flumazenil — benzodiazepine antagonist; risk of seizures in chronic users or TCA co-ingestion; use cautiously. Drug antagonism forms the basis of many antidotes — atropine + pralidoxime (OPC), naloxone (opioid), flumazenil (benzodiazepine), protamine (heparin), vitamin K (warfarin), idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet alfa (rivaroxaban/apixaban), digoxin Fab (digoxin), fomepizole (methanol/ethylene glycol), hydroxocobalamin (cyanide), methylene blue (methaemoglobinaemia), N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol — restores glutathione).

Introduction

Skeletal muscle relaxants are drugs that reduce skeletal muscle tone & spasm. Two broad categories:

  • Neuromuscular blockers — act at NMJ; produce paralysis (used in anaesthesia, intubation); e.g., succinylcholine, vecuronium.
  • Spasmolytics (centrally & peripherally acting) — reduce muscle spasm without paralysis; used for spasticity, muscle spasms, anxiety.

Centrally Acting Skeletal Muscle Relaxants

Act on the CNS (brainstem, spinal cord) to reduce muscle tone by enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA, glycine) or inhibiting excitatory pathways.

Classification

  1. Mephenesin group — Mephenesin, Chlorphenesin, Methocarbamol, Chlorzoxazone (older; mostly replaced).
  2. Benzodiazepines — Diazepam, Lorazepam (GABA-A positive modulators).
  3. α2-Adrenergic agonists — Tizanidine, Clonidine, Dexmedetomidine.
  4. GABA-B agonists — Baclofen.
  5. Other central — Cyclobenzaprine (TCA-like structure), Eperisone, Thiocolchicoside.

Individual Drugs

1. Diazepam (Benzodiazepine)

  • Mechanism — binds to benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptor → ↑ frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening → ↑ inhibitory neurotransmission → ↓ muscle tone & spinal reflexes; also anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant.
  • Uses — muscle spasm (acute); anxiety; alcohol withdrawal; status epilepticus; spasticity (cerebral palsy, MS); tetanus.
  • Dose — 2–10 mg PO TID; 5–10 mg IV (status epilepticus, spasm).
  • Adverse effects — sedation, drowsiness, dependence, tolerance, hypotension (IV), respiratory depression (IV).

2. Baclofen (GABA-B Agonist)

  • Mechanism — agonist at GABA-B receptor (Gi/Go-coupled) → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx & ↑ K⁺ efflux → ↓ release of excitatory transmitters (glutamate, aspartate) in spinal cord & brain → ↓ muscle tone & spasticity.
  • Uses:
    • Spasticity (spinal origin — multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury; cerebral origin — cerebral palsy, stroke less effective).
    • Intrathecal baclofen — severe spasticity unresponsive to oral; programmable pump.
    • Trigeminal neuralgia (adjunct).
    • Alcohol withdrawal (off-label).
    • Gastroesophageal reflux (lower esophageal sphincter relaxation).
  • Dose — 5 mg PO TID, titrate to 20 mg TID/QID (max 80 mg/day); intrathecal 50–2000 µg/day.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, drowsiness, confusion, dizziness, weakness, ataxia, hypotonia; abrupt withdrawal → seizures, hallucinations, hyperthermia; intrathecal — overdose → respiratory depression, coma (antidote — physostigmine, supportive).

3. Tizanidine (α2-Adrenergic Agonist)

  • Mechanism — α2-adrenergic agonist (central) → ↑ presynaptic inhibition of motor neuron excitability → ↓ spasticity; less hypotension than clonidine (more selective α2A at spinal cord).
  • Uses:
    • Spasticity (multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, stroke; less effective than baclofen for severe).
    • Muscle spasm (acute).
    • Headache (tension, migraine — off-label).
  • Dose — 2–4 mg PO every 6–8 h (max 36 mg/day).
  • Adverse effects — sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, hypotension, dry mouth, weakness; hepatotoxicity (rare — monitor LFT); hallucinations; bradycardia.
  • Drug interactions — CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) ↑ tizanidine levels → severe hypotension; contraindicated.

4. Cyclobenzaprine (TCA-Like)

  • Mechanism — structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants; acts at brainstem & spinal cord → ↓ somatic motor activity; anticholinergic; serotonin/norepinephrine effects.
  • Uses — acute muscle spasm (2–3 weeks); fibromyalgia (off-label); not for spasticity (chronic CNS disorders).
  • Dose — 5–10 mg PO TID (max 30 mg/day); extended-release 15–30 mg daily.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation), confusion (elderly); arrhythmias; avoid in elderly, cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

5. Methocarbamol

  • Mechanism — central action (sedation); no direct action on muscle; GABA-A effects.
  • Uses — acute muscle spasm; tetanus; IV for severe spasm.
  • Dose — 1.5 g PO QID initially, then 1 g QID; IV 1–3 g (max 4.5 g/day first day).
  • Adverse effects — sedation, dizziness, hypotension (IV), bradycardia, brown/black discoloration of urine (harmless); avoid IV in renal disease (may precipitate).

6. Chlorzoxazone

  • Mechanism — acts on spinal cord & subcortical brain → ↓ muscle tone.
  • Uses — acute muscle spasm.
  • Dose — 250–500 mg PO TID/QID.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, dizziness, GI upset; hepatotoxicity (rare — boxed warning).

7. Thiocolchicoside

  • Mechanism — GABA-A & glycine receptor antagonist (paradoxically — thought to act centrally as muscle relaxant); anti-inflammatory.
  • Uses — muscle spasm (acute); orthopaedic, rheumatological.
  • Dose — 4–8 mg PO BD; IM 4 mg every 12 h.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, GI upset; seizures (avoid in epilepsy).

8. Eperisone

  • Mechanism — central & peripheral; ↓ γ-motor neuron activity; vasodilator; no sedation.
  • Uses — muscle spasm in cervical spondylosis, shoulder periarthritis, low back pain.
  • Dose — 50 mg PO TID.
  • Adverse effects — dizziness, GI upset; minimal sedation.

9. Other Centrally Acting

  • Orphenadrine — anticholinergic + NMDA antagonist; Parkinsonism & muscle spasm.
  • Carisoprodol — GABA-A effects; metabolised to meprobamate (dependence potential); abuse risk; withdrawn in many countries.
  • Metaxalone — mechanism unclear; sedation.
  • Chlormezanone — withdrawn (severe skin reactions).

Comparison

BaclofenGABA-B agonistSpasticity (spinal > cerebral)Sedation; withdrawal seizures

ThiocolchicosideGABA-A/glycine antagonistAcute spasm (orthopaedic)Seizures
EperisoneCentral + vasodilatorCervical/lumbar painMinimal sedation

Clinical Uses

  • Acute muscle spasm — musculoskeletal injury, strain, sprain; short course (1–2 weeks) — cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, chlorzoxazone, diazepam, thiocolchicoside.
  • Spasticity (chronic CNS disorders):
    • Spinal origin (MS, spinal cord injury) — baclofen (oral or intrathecal), tizanidine.
    • Cerebral origin (cerebral palsy, stroke, traumatic brain injury) — less responsive; baclofen, diazepam, tizanidine; botulinum toxin for focal.
  • Tetanus — IV diazepam, methocarbamol; severe cases — vecuronium + mechanical ventilation.
  • Stiff-person syndrome — diazepam, baclofen, IVIG.
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — dantrolene (peripherally acting); bromocriptine (dopamine agonist).
  • Malignant hyperthermia — dantrolene (only drug; ryanodine receptor antagonist).

Adverse Effects (Common to All Centrally Acting)

  • Sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, lightheadedness.
  • Weakness, ataxia, incoordination.
  • Cognitive impairment, confusion (especially elderly).
  • Paradoxical excitement (children, elderly).
  • Dependence, tolerance (benzodiazepines, carisoprodol).
  • Hypotension (tizanidine, IV methocarbamol).
  • Anticholinergic (cyclobenzaprine).
  • Hepatotoxicity (chlorzoxazone, tizanidine).
  • Withdrawal — abrupt cessation of baclofen → seizures, hallucinations; taper gradually.

Clinical Pearl

Centrally acting muscle relaxants are sedatives — not truly muscle-specific; they reduce muscle tone by generalised CNS depression. For acute muscle spasm (orthopaedic injury) — cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, thiocolchicoside; short course (1–2 weeks); combine with NSAIDs & physical therapy. For chronic spasticity (MS, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy) — baclofen (oral or intrathecal) is drug of choice for spinal spasticity; tizanidine for cerebral & spinal; diazepam for severe. Intrathecal baclofen pump — for severe spasticity unresponsive to oral; programmable; highly effective; risk of overdose (respiratory depression) & withdrawal (seizures, fever, rhabdomyolysis). Tizanidine — avoid with CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) → severe hypotension; check LFT; less hypotension than clonidine. Cyclobenzaprine — structurally TCA; avoid in elderly, cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH (anticholinergic); short-term only. Always taper baclofen — abrupt withdrawal causes seizures, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis (life-threatening). Botulinum toxin — for focal spasticity (cerebral palsy, stroke, dystonia); local injection; lasts 3 months; preferred for focal over generalised spasticity. Dantrolene — peripherally acting (ryanodine receptor antagonist); only drug for malignant hyperthermia & NMS; acts directly on skeletal muscle (no sedation). Introduction

β-Adrenergic blockers (β-blockers) competitively block β-adrenergic receptors (β1, β2, β3); drugs ending in "-olol". Therapeutic uses span cardiovascular, neurological, endocrine, ophthalmological, and psychiatric indications.

Classification

  • Non-selective (β1 + β2) — Propranolol, Timolol, Nadolol, Sotalol (also class III antiarrhythmic), Pindolol (ISA), Oxprenolol (ISA).
  • Cardioselective (β1-selective) — Atenolol, Metoprolol, Bisoprolol, Nebivolol (also NO release), Acebutolol (ISA), Betaxolol, Esmolol (ultra-short-acting IV).
  • Non-selective with α1-blockade — Carvedilol, Labetalol (α1:β ratio 1:3 oral, 1:7 IV), Bucindolol.
  • With ISA (intrinsic sympathomimetic activity) — Pindolol, Acebutolol, Oxprenolol (less bradycardia, less lipid effect).
  • With NO release — Nebivolol (vasodilation via eNOS).

Therapeutic Uses

1. Cardiovascular — Most Important

a. Hypertension
  • First-line (less preferred than ACEI/ARB, CCB, thiazide per recent guidelines).
  • Especially in — hypertension with angina, post-MI, heart failure, AF, migraine, essential tremor, hyperthyroidism, pregnancy (labetalol).
  • Drugs — atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol, labetalol.
  • Mechanism — ↓ cardiac output, ↓ renin release (β1 on JG cells), ↓ central sympathetic outflow, reset baroreceptor.
b. Ischemic heart disease (Angina, MI, Post-MI)
  • Stable angina — ↓ HR, contractility, BP → ↓ myocardial oxygen demand; first-line prophylaxis.
  • Acute MI — IV metoprolol, esmolol; ↓ infarct size, mortality, arrhythmias, reinfarction (if no contraindication — heart failure, hypotension, bradycardia, AV block, severe asthma).
  • Post-MI secondary prevention — lifelong; ↓ mortality ~25%; metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol, propranolol.
  • Avoid — non-DHP CCB (verapamil, diltiazem) combination (bradycardia, AV block).
c. Heart Failure (Systolic — HFrEF)
  • One of four disease-modifying drugs (with ACEI/ARB/ARNI, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor).
  • Start low, go slow, aim high (target dose).
  • Evidence-based β-blockers — Bisoprolol, Carvedilol, Metoprolol succinate (extended-release), Nebivolol (in elderly ≥70 yr — SENIORS trial).
  • Mechanism — counteracts sympathetic overactivation; up-regulates β-receptors; antiarrhythmic; reduces remodelling; improves mortality ~35%.
  • Contraindications — decompensated HF, severe asthma, advanced AV block, symptomatic bradycardia.
  • Not used — propranolol, atenolol, labetalol (no mortality benefit).
d. Arrhythmias
  • Atrial fibrillation / flutter — rate control (↓ AV nodal conduction); IV esmolol, metoprolol for acute; oral for chronic.
  • Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) — terminate (IV); prevent recurrence.
  • Ventricular arrhythmias — adjunct; post-MI; long QT syndrome (propranolol); catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (CPVT).
  • Sotalol — class II + III antiarrhythmic; AF, VT (proarrhythmic risk — QT prolongation, torsades).
e. Aortic dissection
  • Acute — IV labetalol (α1 + β); target SBP 100–120 mmHg, HR 60–80.
  • Chronic — oral labetalol, metoprolol.
f. Marfan syndrome & aortic aneurysm
  • Slow aortic root dilation — propranolol, atenolol; ↓ HR & BP.
g. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)
  • β-blocker (propranolol, metoprolol) — ↓ outflow gradient, ↓ symptoms (dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope).
h. Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS)
  • Propranolol low dose; ↓ HR.
i. Long QT syndrome (congenital)
  • Propranolol — ↓ arrhythmia risk; standard treatment before ICD.

2. Neurological

a. Migraine prophylaxis
  • Propranolol 40–160 mg/day, metoprolol, timolol (FDA-approved); ↓ frequency & severity.
b. Essential tremor
  • Propranolol 40–320 mg/day; ↓ tremor amplitude; mechanism — peripheral β2 blockade in muscle spindles.
c. Anxiety (performance/situational)
  • Propranolol 10–40 mg PRN; ↓ somatic symptoms (palpitations, tremor); no effect on psychic anxiety.
d. Alcohol withdrawal
  • Adjunct; ↓ adrenergic symptoms (CIWA-Ar); not first-line (benzodiazepines); caution — may mask delirium tremens severity.
e. Parkinsonian tremor (adjunct)
  • Propranolol — may reduce tremor.

3. Endocrine

a. Hyperthyroidism / Thyrotoxicosis
  • Propranolol — symptomatic relief (↓ HR, tremor, anxiety, heat intolerance); also inhibits peripheral T4 → T3 conversion (high doses).
  • Thyroid storm — IV propranolol 1 mg/min (with PTU/PTU, iodine, steroids); titrate to HR <100.
  • Preparation for thyroid surgery — propranolol ± iodine.

4. Ophthalmology — Glaucoma

  • Topical β-blockers — ↓ aqueous humour production (↓ cAMP in ciliary epithelium).
  • Timolol (most common), Betaxolol (β1-selective — safer in asthma), Levobunolol, Carteolol (ISA), Metipranolol.
  • Open-angle glaucoma; once or twice daily.
  • Systemic absorption — may cause bronchospasm, bradycardia (especially timolol).

5. Gastrointestinal

a. Portal hypertension (variceal bleeding prophylaxis)
  • Propranolol, nadolol — ↓ portal pressure (↓ cardiac output + splanchnic vasoconstriction via unopposed α); primary & secondary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding.
  • Target — HR 25% below baseline or 55–60 bpm.
  • Carvedilol — preferred for portal hypertension (additional α1-blockade ↓ portal pressure more).

6. Psychiatric / Behavioural

a. Aggression, violent behaviour
  • Propranolol — ↓ impulsivity; especially in intellectual disability, dementia, TBI.
b. Antipsychotic-induced akathisia
  • Propranolol 30–80 mg/day; first-line; mechanism — β2 blockade in CNS.
c. PTSD (adjunct)
  • Propranolol — may reduce reconsolidation of traumatic memories (controversial).

7. Other

a. Restless leg syndrome
  • Adjunct; unclear mechanism.
b. Infantile haemangioma
  • Propranolol 2–3 mg/kg/day — first-line; induces regression; mechanism — vasoconstriction, apoptosis, ↓ VEGF.

AnginaAtenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol

Adverse Effects

  • Cardiac — bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, worsening heart failure (in decompensated HF), rebound hypertension/angina on abrupt withdrawal.
  • Respiratory — bronchospasm (β2 blockade — non-selective more; even cardioselective at high doses); avoid in asthma/severe COPD.
  • Metabolic — mask hypoglycaemia symptoms (except sweating); ↓ insulin release; ↑ triglycerides, ↓ HDL; interfere with insulin/glucose response (less with carvedilol, nebivolol).
  • CNS — fatigue, depression, sleep disturbances, nightmares, hallucinations (lipophilic — propranolol, metoprolol; less with hydrophilic — atenolol).
  • Sexual dysfunction — erectile dysfunction, ↓ libido.
  • Peripheral vascular — cold extremities, Raynaud's phenomenon worsening, claudication (β2 blockade → vasoconstriction).
  • GI — nausea, diarrhoea, constipation.
  • Skin — rash, psoriasis exacerbation (β-blocker-induced).
  • Eye — dry eyes, visual disturbance.
  • Other — antibody formation (Lupus-like with practolol — withdrawn); hepatotoxicity (rare).

Contraindications

  • Severe asthma, severe COPD with reversibility.
  • 2nd or 3rd degree AV block (without pacemaker).
  • Sinus bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome.
  • Decompensated heart failure (until stable).
  • Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg).
  • Severe peripheral arterial disease (claudication).
  • Pheochromocytoma (without α-blockade first — unopposed α → hypertensive crisis).
  • Hypersensitivity.
  • Cardiogenic shock.

Drug Interactions

  • CYP2D6 inhibitors — paroxetine, fluoxetine, quinidine — ↑ levels of metoprolol, carvedilol, propranolol, nebivolol.
  • Non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) — additive bradycardia, AV block; avoid combination.
  • Digoxin — additive bradycardia, AV block.
  • Insulin & oral hypoglycaemics — mask hypoglycaemia symptoms (except sweating); ↓ insulin release; need glucose monitoring.
  • NSAIDs — ↓ antihypertensive effect (prostaglandin inhibition).
  • Clonidine — abrupt cessation of clonidine on β-blocker → severe hypertension (unopposed α).
  • Lidocaine — ↑ levels (↓ hepatic blood flow).
  • Warfarin — ↓ metabolism of R-warfarin (propranolol).
  • Alcohol — additive hypotension.

Withdrawal

  • Abrupt cessation → rebound hypertension, tachycardia, angina, MI, arrhythmias (up-regulation of β-receptors).
  • Always taper gradually over 1–2 weeks.
  • Higher risk with — high doses, long-term use, ischaemic heart disease.

Clinical Pearl

β-blockers are among the most versatile cardiovascular drugs — used for hypertension, angina, post-MI, heart failure, arrhythmias, and many non-cardiovascular conditions. For heart failure (HFrEF) — only bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol have proven mortality benefit; start low (e.g., carvedilol 3.125 mg BD), go slow (double every 2 weeks), aim high (target dose — carvedilol 25 mg BD, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, metoprolol 200 mg daily). Avoid abrupt cessation — rebound hypertension, tachycardia, MI (up-regulated β-receptors); taper over 1–2 weeks. Always give α-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) before β-blocker in phaeochromocytoma — unopposed α → hypertensive crisis. Avoid non-selective β-blockers (propranolol) in asthma — β2 blockade → bronchospasm; use cardioselective (atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol) cautiously if needed. β-blockers mask hypoglycaemia symptoms (tremor, palpitations) except sweating — caution in diabetics on insulin/sulfonylureas; educate patient. Nebivolol — most β1-selective; NO-mediated vasodilation; preferred in elderly, metabolic syndrome. Carvedilol — α1 + β blockade; preferred in HFrEF & hypertension with heart failure; better metabolic profile. Esmolol — ultra-short-acting (half-life 9 min); IV; for SVT, AF rate control in perioperative setting; titratable. Sotalol — class II + III antiarrhythmic; QT prolongation — monitor; risk of torsades. Labetalol — α1 + β; pregnancy hypertensive emergency; IV for aortic dissection, eclampsia. Topical timolol for glaucoma — systemic absorption can cause bronchospasm, bradycardia (especially in elderly); use nasolacrimal occlusion.

Definition

Status asthmaticus (acute severe asthma) is a life-threatening exacerbation of asthma that is unresponsive to standard initial treatment (inhaled β2-agonist + ipratropium + systemic corticosteroid). It can progress to respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, and death. Severe acute asthma without response to initial therapy is also called "acute severe asthma" or "refractory asthma".

Assessment — Severity

Parameter Moderate Severe Life-threatening
PEF50–75% predicted33–50% predicted<33%
SpO₂≥92%<92%<92% + ↓ conscious level
SpeechNormalSentencesWords / unable
RR↑≥25/minBradypnoea / exhaustion
HR≤110/min≥110/minBradycardia / arrhythmia
Use of accessory muscles±+Silent chest / cyanosis
PaO₂ (kPa)Normal<8<8
PaCO₂ (kPa)<4.6<6≥6 (rising)

Signs of Imminent Respiratory Arrest

  • Silent chest (no breath sounds despite effort).
  • Cyanosis, SpO₂ <92% despite O₂.
  • Bradycardia, hypotension.
  • Exhaustion, altered consciousness, confusion, coma.
  • Paradoxical breathing, abdominal breathing.
  • Arrhythmia.

Pharmacotherapy

1. Oxygen

  • 100% oxygen via face mask (or nasal cannula at high flow) to maintain SpO₂ >94% (or 91–95% in COPD overlap).
  • Target PaO₂ >60 mmHg (8 kPa).
  • Monitor — pulse oximetry, ABG.

2. Short-Acting β2-Agonists (SABA) — First-Line

  • Salbutamol (albuterol):
    • Nebulised — 2.5–5 mg (5 mg in severe) every 20 min × 3 doses in first hour; then 5–10 mg every hour or continuous nebulisation (10–15 mg/h).
    • MDI with spacer — 4–8 puffs (100 µg each) every 20 min × 3 doses; suitable for less severe.
    • IV (rarely needed) — 5 µg/kg loading over 10 min, then 0.1–0.2 µg/kg/min infusion; titrate to effect; risk of tachycardia, hypokalaemia, lactic acidosis.
    • Mechanism — β2 agonist → ↑ cAMP → bronchodilation; relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, inhibits mast cell mediator release, ↑ mucociliary clearance.
  • Levosalbutamol (R-salbutamol) — active enantiomer; 1.25–2.5 mg nebulised; may have fewer side effects.
  • Terbutaline — alternative; 5–10 mg nebulised; SC 0.25 mg.

3. Anticholinergics — Added to SABA

  • Ipratropium bromide:
    • Nebulised — 0.5 mg every 20 min × 3 doses in first hour; then 0.5 mg every 4–6 h.
    • MDI with spacer — 4–8 puffs every 20 min × 3 doses.
    • Mechanism — muscarinic (M3) antagonist → ↓ cGMP → bronchodilation; reduces mucus secretion; additive to SABA.
  • Combination — salbutamol 2.5 mg + ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised every 20 min × 3 (Combivent); preferred in severe.

4. Systemic Corticosteroids — Essential for All Severe Exacerbations

  • Reduce inflammation, oedema, mucus; prevent relapse; onset 4–6 h.
  • Hydrocortisone — 100–200 mg IV every 6 h (loading 4 mg/kg); preferred for severe / unable to take oral.
  • Methylprednisolone — 40–60 mg IV every 6 h (or 1–2 mg/kg/day); alternative.
  • Prednisolone — 40–60 mg PO daily (if tolerating oral); equivalent efficacy to IV.
  • Duration — 5–10 days; taper not necessary for short course.
  • Early administration (within 1 h) reduces hospitalisation & mortality.

5. Magnesium Sulphate — Adjunct for Severe

  • IV Magnesium sulphate — 2 g (1–2 g) IV over 20 min (in adults; 25–50 mg/kg in children max 2 g); bronchodilator (inhibits Ca²⁺ influx, stabilises mast cells).
  • Indications — severe exacerbation not responding to SABA + ipratropium + steroid; PEF <50% predicted; life-threatening features.
  • Adverse effects — flushing, hypotension, weakness; monitor BP, reflexes; avoid in renal failure (or reduce dose).
  • Nebulised magnesium (isotonic) — 3 × 500 mg doses in first hour; less effective than IV but no systemic effects.

6. Methylxanthines — Second-Line (Historical)

  • IV Aminophylline:
    • 5 mg/kg loading over 20 min (if not on theophylline); then 0.5–0.7 mg/kg/h infusion.
    • Monitor serum theophylline (target 10–15 µg/mL); narrow therapeutic window.
    • Less effective than SABA; more adverse effects (arrhythmia, seizures, GI); rarely used now; reserved for refractory.
  • Theophylline (oral) — for chronic; not for acute severe.

7. Ketamine — Adjunct / Anaesthetic

  • Dissociative anaesthetic with bronchodilator properties.
  • IV 0.5–1 mg/kg loading then 0.5–2 mg/kg/h infusion.
  • Useful for — severe bronchospasm requiring intubation; facilitates intubation without compromising bronchodilation.
  • Adverse — hypertension, tachycardia, emergence reactions, increased secretions (combine with antisialogogue).

8. Heliox — Adjunct

  • Helium-oxygen mixture (80:20 or 70:30) — lower density than air → reduces work of breathing; improves airflow in narrowed airways (laminar flow).
  • Useful for — severe airflow obstruction not responding to standard therapy; bridge to mechanical ventilation.
  • Limited by — need for >30% oxygen (heliox requires >20% oxygen minimum).

9. Inhalational Anaesthetics — Last Resort

  • Isoflurane, sevoflurane, halothane, enflurane — bronchodilator; useful in refractory status asthmaticus on mechanical ventilation.
  • Administered via anaesthesia machine; intensive monitoring; ICU.
  • Adverse — hypotension, arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia (halothane).

10. Other Adjuncts

  • Antibiotics — only if bacterial infection suspected (fever, purulent sputum, infiltrate on X-ray); not routine.
  • Sedation — for intubated patients; propofol, midazolam, fentanyl (avoid histamine-releasing — morphine, meperidine).
  • Neuromuscular blockade — vecuronium, rocuronium; for ventilator dyssynchrony.
  • Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) — for refractory hypercapnia/hypoxaemia; last resort.
  • Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) — IV preparation (in trials); role unclear.
  • Anti-IgE (omalizumab), anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab, benralizumab), anti-IL-4Rα (dupilumab) — for chronic severe eosinophilic asthma; not for acute.

Non-Pharmacological Management

  • Mechanical ventilation — for respiratory failure, exhaustion, altered consciousness; permissive hypercapnia (low tidal volume 4–8 mL/kg, slow rate 10–14/min, short inspiratory time, long expiratory time to avoid air-trapping); deep sedation ± paralysis.
  • Non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) — controversial; may benefit carefully selected patients with hypercapnia but risk of deterioration.
  • Fluids — IV fluids to maintain hydration (may be needed due to poor intake, tachypnoea); avoid overload (pulmonary oedema).
  • Electrolytes — correct hypokalaemia (β2-agonist effect), hypomagnesaemia.
  • Monitoring — continuous SpO₂, ECG, BP, PEF (if cooperative), ABG; watch for fatigue, silent chest, hypercapnia.

Triggers to Identify & Treat

  • Respiratory infection (viral URI — rhinovirus, RSV, influenza; bacterial).
  • Allergen exposure — dust mites, pollen, animal dander, mould.
  • Non-compliance with controller medication (ICS).
  • NSAIDs, β-blockers, aspirin (in susceptible patients).
  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
  • Exercise, cold air, emotional stress.
  • Smoking (active or passive).
  • Occupational exposure.
  • Food additives — sulfites.

Discharge & Follow-Up

  • Continue prednisolone 40–60 mg/day for 5–10 days.
  • Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) — long-acting; beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone, ciclesonide; the cornerstone of chronic therapy.
  • ICS + LABA (long-acting β2-agonist) — combination inhaler (fluticasone + salmeterol; budesonide + formoterol); for moderate-severe persistent asthma.
  • SABA — reliever; salbutamol MDI for symptom relief.
  • Asthma action plan — written; peak flow monitoring; recognise & respond to exacerbations.
  • Follow-up — within 1–4 weeks; assess control; adjust stepwise.
  • Education — inhaler technique; trigger avoidance; smoking cessation; vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal).

Clinical Pearl

Status asthmaticus is a medical emergency — recognise severity early (PEF, SpO₂, speech, RR, HR, ABG); silent chest & rising PaCO₂ are signs of impending arrest. First-line therapy: 100% oxygen + nebulised salbutamol (5 mg) + ipratropium (0.5 mg) every 20 min × 3 doses + systemic corticosteroid (hydrocortisone 100–200 mg IV or prednisolone 40–60 mg PO). IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 20 min for severe unresponsive cases — bronchodilator; well-tolerated. Avoid IV aminophylline if possible — narrow therapeutic index, seizures, arrhythmia; less effective than SABA. Indications for intubation — altered consciousness, exhaustion, silent chest, PaCO₂ rising (>45 mmHg), severe hypoxaemia despite maximal therapy. Mechanical ventilation strategy — permissive hypercapnia (low tidal volume 6 mL/kg, slow rate 10/min, long expiratory time); avoid air-trapping (auto-PEEP); deep sedation ± paralysis. Nebulised salbutamol continues during mechanical ventilation — inline nebuliser in circuit. Inhalational anaesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane) — refractory cases; bronchodilator; ICU with anaesthesia machine. ECMO — last resort; refractory hypercapnia/hypoxaemia. Always identify & treat trigger — infection (antibiotics only if bacterial), allergen, NSAID, non-compliance. Discharge on ICS (or ICS + LABA) + SABA reliever + 5-day prednisolone + asthma action plan + follow-up. India — asthma mortality high; access to ICS limited; overuse of SABA & underuse of ICS; affordability & education critical. Asthma deaths are largely preventable with proper chronic controller therapy (ICS) & early aggressive treatment of exacerbations.

Introduction

Acute iron poisoning is a life-threatening overdose, especially in children (accidental ingestion of iron tablets — often mistaken for sweets). Severity depends on dose — <20 mg/kg elemental iron generally asymptomatic; 20–40 mg/kg mild-moderate; 40–60 mg/kg moderate-severe; >60 mg/kg potentially lethal.

Pathophysiology

  1. Local corrosive effect on GI mucosa — free iron (especially ferrous sulphate) is directly toxic to gastric & intestinal epithelium → vomiting, diarrhoea, haemorrhage, fluid loss.
  2. Systemic toxicity — absorbed iron exceeds transferrin binding capacity → free iron in plasma → enters cells → damages mitochondria → inhibits oxidative phosphorylation → metabolic acidosis, hepatotoxicity, coagulopathy, shock.
  3. Free iron:
    • ↑ Capillary permeability → vasodilation → hypotension, shock.
    • Direct cardiotoxicity → negative inotropy.
    • Hepatocyte necrosis — free iron causes lipid peroxidation & mitochondrial damage.
    • Inhibits thrombin generation → coagulopathy.
    • Metabolic acidosis — ↓ aerobic metabolism → ↑ lactate; iron itself is acid (ferrous sulphate); releases H⁺.

Clinical Stages (4 stages)

Stage 1 — Gastrointestinal (0.5–6 h after ingestion)

  • Direct corrosive effect on GI mucosa.
  • Symptoms — vomiting (often bloody), abdominal pain, diarrhoea (often bloody), haematemesis, melena.
  • Signs — dehydration, hypovolaemic shock, lethargy, metabolic acidosis (early).
  • Severe cases — hypotension, tachycardia.
  • Most deaths occur in this stage if untreated.

Stage 2 — Latent / Apparent Improvement (6–24 h)

  • Apparent clinical improvement (deceptive).
  • GI symptoms resolve; patient looks better.
  • BUT — ongoing systemic absorption, metabolic acidosis, hepatotoxicity developing.
  • Caution — do not discharge; this is a "quiescent phase" before stage 3.
  • Laboratory — rising serum iron, metabolic acidosis, leukocytosis, hyperglycaemia.

Stage 3 — Systemic Toxicity / Shock (12–48 h)

  • Severe metabolic acidosis, shock.
  • Hepatotoxicity — central lobular necrosis; ↑ AST, ALT; coagulopathy; jaundice; hepatic failure (most common cause of death).
  • Cardiovascular — myocardial depression, arrhythmias, refractory shock.
  • CNS — lethargy, coma, seizures.
  • Metabolic — severe metabolic acidosis (↑ anion gap), hypoglycaemia (later hyperglycaemia), hypocalcaemia.
  • Coagulopathy — ↓ thrombin, ↓ clotting factors; bleeding.
  • Renal failure — acute tubular necrosis.
  • Mortality 10–50% in severe cases.

Stage 4 — Late / Obstructive (2–6 weeks)

  • GI obstruction / stricture — at pylorus, gastric antrum, duodenum (from corrosive scarring).
  • Symptoms — early satiety, vomiting, weight loss.
  • Requires endoscopic dilation or surgical correction.

Diagnosis

  • History — type of iron preparation (ferrous sulphate, fumarate, gluconate); number of tablets; time of ingestion; weight of patient.
  • Calculate elemental iron dose:
    • Ferrous sulphate — 20% elemental iron (325 mg tablet = 65 mg elemental iron).
    • Ferrous fumarate — 33% (325 mg = 107 mg elemental).
    • Ferrous gluconate — 12% (325 mg = 39 mg elemental).
    • Polysaccharide iron complex — 100%.
    • Multivitamins with iron — variable.
  • Serum iron level — peak 2–6 h (up to 8 h for extended-release); >350 µg/dL symptomatic; >500 µg/dL severe; >1000 µg/dL potentially lethal.
  • Total iron binding capacity (TIBC) — historically used; iron/TIBC ratio >1 suggests toxicity; not reliable in acute setting (TIBC changes slowly).
  • Abdominal X-ray — radio-opaque tablets in stomach/intestine (60% of tablets visible); guides decontamination.
  • Laboratory:
    • ABG — metabolic acidosis (high anion gap).
    • CBG — leukocytosis (>15,000/µL suggests significant poisoning); hyperglycaemia.
    • LFT — ↑ AST, ALT (hepatotoxicity); coagulation — PT/INR, aPTT.
    • Renal function — urea, creatinine.
    • Glucose — hyperglycaemia initially, hypoglycaemia later.
    • Lactate — elevated.
    • Urinalysis — for crystals, haematuria.
  • Deferoxamine challenge test (historical) — IM deferoxamine 50 mg/kg; if "vin rose" urine appears, indicates free iron; replaced by serum iron level.

Management

1. Supportive Care

  • Airway, breathing, circulation — IV access, fluid resuscitation, oxygen.
  • Correct hypovolaemia, acidosis (sodium bicarbonate if pH <7.2), hypoglycaemia.
  • Treat seizures — diazepam, lorazepam.
  • Treat arrhythmias — standard ACLS.
  • Blood transfusion if significant GI haemorrhage.
  • Monitor — continuous ECG, BP, SpO₂; serial iron levels, LFT, ABG, coagulation.

2. Gastrointestinal Decontamination

  • Activated charcoal — INEFFECTIVE for iron (does not adsorb iron); do not give.
  • Gastric lavage — if recent ingestion (<1 h) & tablets visible on X-ray; large-bore orogastric tube.
  • Whole bowel irrigation (WBI) — polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution 1.5–2 L/h in adults (20–40 mL/kg/h in children) until effluent clear & no tablets on X-ray; for enteric-coated, sustained-release, large ingestion.
  • Endoscopic removal — if tablets in stomach & not passable; for bezoar.
  • Surgical removal — for adherent tablet mass, bezoar unresponsive to WBI.

3. Chelation Therapy — Deferoxamine (DFO, Desferrioxamine)

  • Indications:
    • Serum iron >500 µg/dL (or >350 µg/dL with symptoms).
    • Serum iron >TIBC.
    • Significant symptoms (shock, severe acidosis, lethargy).
    • Abdominal X-ray showing multiple tablets (presumed high ingestion).
    • Peak iron level unknown but significant ingestion (>40 mg/kg elemental).
  • Dose:
    • IV — 15 mg/kg/h initially; may ↑ to 30–40 mg/kg/h if severe; max 6 g/day (or 80 mg/kg/day).
    • IM — 50 mg/kg every 6 h (initial stabilisation; less preferred than IV).
    • Continue until serum iron <300 µg/dL, metabolic acidosis resolves, clinical improvement (typically 12–24 h).
    • Prolonged therapy (>24 h) — risk of pulmonary toxicity (ARDS) and Yersinia enterocolitica infection (iron is growth factor).
  • Mechanism:
    • Deferoxamine binds free iron in plasma (1:1 molar ratio — 100 mg DFO binds 8.5 mg elemental iron).
    • Forms ferrioxamine — water-soluble complex; excreted in urine (red-orange "vin rose" urine).
    • Does NOT bind iron in transferrin, haemoglobin, or cytochromes — only free iron.
  • Adverse effects:
    • Hypotension (rapid IV infusion) — slow rate.
    • Allergic reactions (rash, anaphylaxis).
    • Pulmonary toxicity — ARDS if prolonged (>24 h) at high doses.
    • Yersinia enterocolitica infection — ferrioxamine is growth factor for Yersinia; monitor for fever, diarrhoea, abdominal pain; treat with fluoroquinolone, TMP-SMX.
    • Renal & hepatic dysfunction (rare).
    • Visual & auditory toxicity (chronic therapy).
    • Acute lung injury, hypotension, anaphylaxis.

4. Other Chelators

  • Deferasirox — oral; chronic iron overload; less effective in acute poisoning; not first-line for acute.
  • Deferiprone — oral; chronic; can cross cell membrane (may remove intracellular iron).
  • These oral chelators are NOT used in acute iron poisoning — DFO remains standard.

5. Exchange Transfusion / Haemodialysis

  • Exchange transfusion — for massive poisoning, especially in children; removes iron-ferrioxamine complex.
  • Haemodialysis — ineffective (iron-protein complex too large); not indicated for iron removal; may be needed for renal failure.

  • Serum iron >500 µg/dL.
  • Symptomatic (shock, acidosis, altered consciousness, severe GI symptoms).
  • Requiring deferoxamine infusion.
  • Significant metabolic acidosis.
  • Coagulopathy, hepatic dysfunction.
  • Cardiovascular instability.

  • Child-resistant packaging (blister packs are NOT child-proof).
  • Store iron tablets out of reach of children.
  • Education — accidental ingestion is most common in children <6 years.
  • Reduce tablet count in pregnancy prescriptions.
  • Use sustained-release formulations (slower absorption, lower peak).
  • Public awareness — iron tablets look like sweets.

Clinical Pearl

Acute iron poisoning is most common in children who mistake iron tablets for sweets — pregnant women's iron tablets are the typical source. Calculate elemental iron dose — ferrous sulphate is 20% elemental iron (325 mg tablet = 65 mg elemental); ferrous fumarate 33%; ferrous gluconate 12%. Dose >40 mg/kg elemental iron is significant; >60 mg/kg potentially lethal. Activated charcoal does NOT bind iron — do NOT give; use gastric lavage or whole bowel irrigation if tablets visible on X-ray. 4-stage clinical course — GI symptoms (stage 1, 0–6 h) → apparent improvement (stage 2, 6–24 h, deceptive) → systemic toxicity with hepatotoxicity, shock, acidosis (stage 3, 12–48 h) → late GI stricture (stage 4, 2–6 weeks). NEVER discharge patient in stage 2 — appearance is deceptive; ongoing absorption & systemic toxicity develop. Deferoxamine (DFO) is the antidote — IV 15 mg/kg/h; binds free iron → ferrioxamine → excreted in urine (red-orange "vin rose"). Indications for DFO — serum iron >500 µg/dL, symptoms, metabolic acidosis. Serum iron peaks at 2–6 h — sample then; levels may be falsely low after peak (redistribution). Abdominal X-ray — radio-opaque tablets (60% visible); guides decontamination. Prolonged DFO (>24 h) causes pulmonary toxicity (ARDS) — balance benefit vs risk. Hepatic failure is most common cause of death — free iron causes central lobular necrosis. Always admit & observe any child with suspected iron ingestion; do not rely on early asymptomatic phase. Prevention is key — child-resistant packaging, education, storage out of reach.

Introduction

Furosemide — a loop diuretic — is one of the most potent diuretics available. Used for oedema (heart failure, renal, hepatic), hypertension, acute pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia, hypercalcaemia, and acute kidney injury. Drug of choice when rapid & potent diuresis is needed.

Chemistry & Classification

  • Sulfonamide derivative; contains sulphonamide group (cross-reactivity with sulfonamide antibiotics — controversial; most patients with sulfonamide antibiotic allergy tolerate furosemide).
  • Loop diuretic — acts on thick ascending limb of loop of Henle.
  • Other loop diuretics — Bumetanide, Torsemide, Ethacrynic acid (NOT sulfonamide — for sulfa allergy), Piretanide, Azosemide.

Mechanism of Action

  1. Inhibits Na-K-2Cl (NKCC2) cotransporter in thick ascending limb of loop of Henle (site of 25% Na⁺ reabsorption).
  2. Acts from luminal side — secreted into proximal tubule via OAT (organic anion transporter); reaches tubular lumen; blocks NKCC2.
  3. ↓ Reabsorption of Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ → ↑ excretion of these ions + water.
  4. Disrupts countercurrent multiplication → loss of medullary hypertonicity → impaired water reabsorption in collecting duct → profound diuresis (high-ceiling diuretic).
  5. Increases Ca²⁺ & Mg²⁺ excretion:
    • ↓ Positive lumen potential (normally maintained by K⁺ back-leak through ROMK) → ↓ paracellular Ca²⁺ & Mg²⁺ reabsorption.
    • Used for hypercalcaemia (with IV hydration).
  6. Vasodilation:
    • Acute (IV) — vasodilation of renal vasculature & peripheral veins; ↓ preload (for acute pulmonary oedema).
    • Stimulates renal prostaglandin (PGE2, PGI2) release → ↑ renal blood flow; redistributes to inner cortex.
    • NSAIDs block this prostaglandin-mediated effect → ↓ diuretic efficacy.
    • ↑ Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) release.
  7. Acute effect on renin — stimulates renin release (via macula densa — ↓ NaCl delivery) → activates RAAS; chronic use increases aldosterone.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Absorption — oral; bioavailability 60–70% (variable 10–100%); onset 30–60 min oral, 5 min IV; peak 1–2 h oral, 20–30 min IV.
  • Protein binding — 95% (albumin); only free drug reaches tubule via OAT.
  • Volume of distribution — 0.1 L/kg; small.
  • Metabolism — partial hepatic glucuronidation; ~50% excreted unchanged in urine.
  • Half-life — 1.5–2 h (longer in renal/hepatic failure).
  • Duration of action — 4–6 h oral; 2 h IV.
  • Crosses placenta; excreted in breast milk (avoid breastfeeding).
  • Elimination — renal (glomerular filtration + OAT secretion) 50%; hepatic (glucuronidation) 50%.

Therapeutic Uses

  1. Acute pulmonary oedema / left ventricular failure — IV furosemide 20–80 mg; rapid venodilation → ↓ preload; then diuresis. Drug of choice for acute decompensated heart failure.
  2. Chronic heart failure (HFrEF) — oral; relieve congestion; titrate to euvolaemia; NOT disease-modifying (does not improve mortality — use with ACEI/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor).
  3. Hypertension — oral; not first-line (thiazide preferred); useful in CKD (GFR <30) where thiazide ineffective; or in resistant hypertension (add to thiazide — sequential nephron blockade).
  4. Renal disease:
    • Acute kidney injury — IV; volume overload; not for prevention of AKI (negative trial — furosemide does not prevent AKI in high-risk).
    • Chronic kidney disease (CKD) — oedema; hypertension; high doses needed (thiazide ineffective at GFR <30); combine with thiazide for synergy.
    • Nephrotic syndrome — high doses ± albumin (controversial).
  5. Hepatic cirrhosis with ascites:
    • Combine with spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) — ratio 40 mg furosemide : 100 mg spironolactone; titrate to weight loss 0.5 kg/day (without oedema) or 1 kg/day (with oedema); monitor Na⁺, K⁺, creatinine.
    • Spironolactone prevents hypokalaemia-induced hepatic encephalopathy (NH₃ absorption ↑ by hypokalaemia).
  6. Hypercalcaemia:
    • IV saline hydration first (to restore intravascular volume & calciuresis); then IV furosemide 20–40 mg every 4–6 h; increases Ca²⁺ excretion.
    • Monitor K⁺, Mg²⁺; replace.
    • Less commonly used now — bisphosphonates, calcitonin, denosumab preferred for hypercalcaemia of malignancy.
  7. Hyperkalaemia — adjunct; promotes K⁺ excretion (with normal saline to maintain volume); not first-line (insulin + dextrose, β2-agonist, calcium for stabilisation; potassium binders — patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate).
  8. SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone) — combined with hypertonic saline; produces hypertonic urine.
  9. Drug overdose — forced diuresis (with saline) for bromide, fluoride, iodide, lithium ( controversial — not recommended for most drugs; haemodialysis preferred).
  10. Cerebral oedema — IV; alternative to mannitol (especially if acute kidney injury); reduces intracranial pressure.
  11. Hyperkalaemia in hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis.
  12. Hypertensive emergency with pulmonary oedema — IV.

Adverse Effects

1. Fluid & Electrolyte

  • Hypokalaemia — ↑ distal Na⁺ delivery → ↑ K⁺ & H⁺ excretion (aldosterone); most common; monitor K⁺; supplement or combine with K-sparing diuretic (spironolactone, amiloride).
  • Hypomagnesaemia — ↑ Mg²⁺ excretion; worsens hypokalaemia (refractory K⁺ repletion needs Mg²⁺ first).
  • Hypocalcaemia — ↑ Ca²⁺ excretion; usually mild.
  • Hyponatraemia — less common than thiazides; free water clearance impaired.
  • Metabolic alkalosis — contraction alkalosis (volume depletion) + H⁺ loss; treat with KCl & volume repletion.
  • Volume depletion / dehydration — hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, prerenal azotaemia.

2. Cardiovascular

  • Hypotension — volume depletion.
  • Arrhythmias — from hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia.
  • Venodilation may worsen shock (avoid in cardiogenic shock without pulmonary oedema).

3. Metabolic

  • Hyperglycaemia — ↓ insulin release (hypokalaemia); ↑ insulin resistance; especially in diabetics; monitor blood glucose.
  • Hyperuricaemia — ↓ renal uric acid excretion (competition with OAT); gout flare; use losartan (uricosuric) if gout.
  • Dyslipidaemia — ↑ triglycerides, ↑ LDL, ↑ total cholesterol (mild; less than thiazides).
  • Increased urea, creatinine — prerenal (volume depletion) or direct (high dose).

4. Ototoxicity

  • Tinnitus, hearing loss, deafness — dose-dependent; more with IV high doses (>4 mg/min); reversible; permanent in severe cases.
  • Mechanism — alteration of ion transport in inner hair cells (NKCC1 in stria vascularis); electrolyte disturbance in endolymph.
  • Risk factors — renal impairment, high doses, rapid IV infusion, concurrent ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cisplatin).
  • Prevention — slow IV infusion (≤4 mg/min); avoid ototoxic combinations.
  • Ethacrynic acid — most ototoxic (avoid).

5. Hypersensitivity

  • Sulfa allergy — rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, anaphylaxis (furosemide is sulfonamide).
  • Cross-reactivity with sulfonamide antibiotics — low (<10%); most patients with sulfonamide antibiotic allergy tolerate furosemide; if true severe sulfa allergy — use ethacrynic acid (not sulfonamide).
  • Photosensitivity.
  • Interstitial nephritis — rare.
  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis — rare.

6. Other

  • GI — nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, pancreatitis (rare).
  • Skew — asymptomatic hyperamylasaemia.
  • Skin — rash, photosensitivity.
  • Hepatic encephalopathy — precipitated by hypokalaemia (in cirrhosis).
  • Thiamine deficiency — chronic use; especially in heart failure; may worsen cardiac function; supplement.
  • Urine incontinence — drug is potent diuretic; dosing timing matters.

Drug Interactions

  • Aminoglycosides — additive ototoxicity & nephrotoxicity; avoid or monitor.
  • Lithium — ↓ lithium excretion (furosemide-induced volume depletion & ↑ proximal tubular reabsorption) → toxicity; monitor lithium levels; avoid or use lowest effective dose with hydration.
  • Digoxin — hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia ↑ digoxin toxicity; monitor K⁺, Mg²⁺.
  • NSAIDs — ↓ diuretic efficacy (prostaglandin inhibition); ↑ renal risk; avoid if possible.
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — first-dose hypotension if volume-depleted; reduce dose or initiate ACEI/ARB after volume status stabilised.
  • Cisplatin, carboplatin — additive ototoxicity & nephrotoxicity.
  • Corticosteroids, amphotericin B, β2-agonists — additive hypokalaemia.
  • Sucralfate — ↓ furosemide absorption; separate doses by 2 h.
  • Phenytoin — ↓ furosemide absorption & effect.
  • Theophylline — furosemide ↑ theophylline levels.
  • Warfarin — displacement from albumin (transient ↑ INR).
  • Baclofen — additive hypotension.

Contraindications

  • Anuria (no urine output).
  • Severe hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypovolaemia, hypotension.
  • Hypersensitivity to sulfonamides (use ethacrynic acid).
  • Severe hepatic coma / pre-coma (risk of precipitating hepatic encephalopathy).
  • Addison's disease (cortisol deficiency; ↑ diuresis → collapse).
  • Renal failure due to nephrotoxic drugs (caution).
  • Pregnancy (avoid; crosses placenta; may cause fetal diuresis, hypovolaemia); use only if clearly needed (pulmonary oedema in pregnancy).
  • Obstructive uropathy (inability to excrete urine).

Comparison of Loop Diuretics

Bumetanide401–1.5 h80–100%More consistent absorption; useful in CKD & intestinal oedema

Clinical Pearl

Furosemide is the drug of choice for acute pulmonary oedema — IV 20–80 mg; rapid venodilation → ↓ preload → symptom relief within 5 min; then diuresis follows. For chronic heart failure — titrate to euvolaemia; NOT disease-modifying (does not improve mortality); always combine with disease-modifying drugs (ACEI/ARB/ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor). For cirrhosis with ascites — combine with spironolactone (40 mg furosemide : 100 mg spironolactone ratio); spironolactone prevents hypokalaemia-induced hepatic encephalopathy; titrate to weight loss 0.5–1 kg/day; monitor Na⁺, K⁺, creatinine. Always monitor K⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺, renal function — hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyponatraemia, prerenal azotaemia common; replace electrolytes. Ototoxicity — IV infusion >4 mg/min increases risk; slow infusion; avoid with aminoglycosides; ethacrynic acid most ototoxic. Sulfa allergy — furosemide is sulfonamide; cross-reactivity with sulfonamide antibiotics is low (<10%); most patients tolerate; if severe sulfa allergy — use ethacrynic acid (not sulfonamide). NSAIDs reduce furosemide efficacy — inhibit renal prostaglandins; avoid or monitor. Lithium interaction — furosemide reduces lithium excretion → toxicity; monitor levels; avoid or use carefully. Thiamine deficiency — chronic furosemide in HF; may worsen cardiac function; supplement (especially in malnourished, alcoholics). Bumetanide & torsemide — more consistent oral bioavailability than furosemide (10–100%); preferred in CKD, intestinal oedema (where furosemide absorption unreliable); torsemide may reduce mortality in HF. Definition

Volume of distribution (Vd) — also called apparent volume of distribution — is defined as the theoretical volume of fluid that would be required to contain the total amount of drug in the body at the same concentration as in plasma, assuming the body to be a single homogeneous compartment.

Mathematically:

Vd = (Dose administered) / (Plasma concentration at time zero, C₀)

Or after IV bolus:

Vd = Dose / C₀

For oral administration: Vd = (Dose × F) / C₀, where F = bioavailability.

Concept of Apparent Volume

  • Vd is a theoretical (apparent) volume — it does NOT correspond to any real anatomical space.
  • It is a pharmacokinetic parameter that describes how widely a drug distributes in the body relative to plasma.
  • Vd reflects the apparent space a drug "appears to occupy" based on plasma concentration.
  • If a drug remains largely in plasma (e.g., highly protein-bound, large molecule), Vd is small (close to plasma volume).
  • If a drug distributes extensively into tissues (e.g., lipid-soluble), Vd is large (may exceed total body water many-fold).

Normal Body Fluid Compartments

Compartment Volume (70 kg adult)
Plasma3 L
Blood5 L
Extracellular fluid (ECF)13–15 L
Total body water (TBW)42 L (60% body weight)

Interpretation of Vd Values

1. Low Vd (3–5 L, close to plasma volume)

  • Drug largely confined to plasma.
  • Reasons — large molecular size, high plasma protein binding, low lipid solubility, low tissue affinity.
  • Examples — heparin (large molecule), warfarin (99% albumin-bound), phenylbutazone, sulphonamides, NSAIDs, furosemide (high protein binding), monoclonal antibodies.
  • Cannot be removed by haemodialysis easily (if high protein binding).

2. Intermediate Vd (10–20 L, close to ECF)

  • Drug distributes in extracellular fluid.
  • Reasons — low lipid solubility, hydrophilic, moderate protein binding.
  • Examples — aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin — polar, hydrophilic), penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin, lithium.
  • Can be removed by haemodialysis.

3. High Vd (>40 L, may exceed body weight many-fold)

  • Drug distributes widely into tissues.
  • Reasons — high lipid solubility, low plasma protein binding, high tissue binding (especially to muscle, fat, brain).
  • Examples — digoxin (Vd ~500 L; binds to Na-K-ATPase in muscle), amiodarone (Vd ~60 L/kg; accumulates in fat), propranolol, tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), chloroquine (Vd ~100 L/kg; melanin binding), quinine, haloperidol, fluoxetine, ivermectin.
  • Vd may be hundreds of litres — this is theoretical (apparent), not real.
  • Not effectively removed by haemodialysis (drug in tissues, not plasma).

Factors Affecting Vd

  1. Lipid solubility — higher lipid solubility → higher Vd (crosses membranes, enters fat, brain).
  2. Plasma protein binding — high binding (albumin) → low Vd (drug stays in plasma); only free (unbound) drug distributes.
  3. Tissue binding — high tissue binding (muscle, fat, melanin, bone) → high Vd (digoxin, chloroquine, tetracycline in bone).
  4. Molecular size — large molecules (heparin, monoclonal antibodies) → low Vd (cannot cross capillary).
  5. Ionisation (pKa) & pH — ionised (charged) drugs do not cross lipid membranes → low Vd; trapping in compartments (pH partition — weak bases accumulate in acidic compartments like lysosomes).
  6. Permeability / blood flow — high blood flow organs (brain, heart, kidney, liver) equilibrate rapidly; low flow (fat, muscle) take longer.
  7. Disease states:
    • Heart failure — ↓ cardiac output, ↓ tissue perfusion → ↓ Vd for some drugs (lidocaine).
    • Uraemia / renal failure — ↓ protein binding (organic acids compete) → ↑ free drug → ↑ Vd for acidic drugs.
    • Cirrhosis — ↓ albumin → ↑ Vd; ascites adds volume → ↑ Vd.
    • Nephrotic syndrome — ↓ albumin → ↑ Vd.
    • Obesity — ↑ Vd for lipophilic drugs (amiodarone, diazepam, verapamil).
    • Pregnancy — ↑ plasma volume → ↑ Vd.
  8. Age:
    • Neonates — ↑ total body water, ↓ fat, immature BBB → higher Vd for water-soluble drugs.
    • Elderly — ↓ total body water, ↓ lean mass, ↑ fat → ↑ Vd for lipophilic drugs (diazepam).

Clinical Significance

  1. Loading dose calculation:
    • For drugs with high Vd or long half-life, loading dose achieves therapeutic plasma concentration rapidly.
    • Loading dose = (Vd × Target plasma concentration) / Bioavailability.
    • Example — digoxin: Vd ~7 L/kg; target 1.5 ng/mL; loading dose = 7 × 1.5 × 70 kg = 735 µg.
    • Amiodarone: loading dose 800–1600 mg/day for 1–3 weeks (large Vd).
  2. Half-life calculation:
    • t½ = (0.693 × Vd) / Clearance.
    • ↑Vd → ↑t½ (longer duration of action); e.g., amiodarone (t½ ~50 days), diazepam (t½ 30–60 h, active metabolite nordazepam ~100 h).
  3. Drug clearance:
    • Clearance = (Rate of elimination) / (Plasma concentration).
    • Vd affects drug dosing interval — high Vd → longer dosing interval.
  4. Predicting dialysability:
    • Low Vd + low protein binding + small molecule → dialysable (lithium, salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, aminoglycosides).
    • High Vd or high protein binding → not effectively dialysable (digoxin, tricyclics, phenytoin, warfarin).
  5. Predicting toxicity & overdose management:
    • High Vd drugs — large tissue stores; not removed by dialysis; may require repeated doses of antidote (e.g., digoxin — use Fab antibody).
    • Low Vd drugs — may respond to dialysis or forced diuresis.
  6. Dose adjustment in disease:
    • Volume overload (heart failure, oedema) — ↑ Vd for some drugs → may need higher dose.
    • Dehydration — ↓ Vd → higher plasma concentration → reduce dose.
  7. Drug selection in special situations:
    • CNS drugs — need to cross BBB; high lipid solubility → high Vd (diazepam, phenytoin, antidepressants).
    • Pregnancy — avoid high Vd drugs (cross placenta).

One-Compartment vs Two-Compartment Models

  • One-compartment model — drug distributes instantaneously & uniformly throughout body; plasma concentration declines monoexponentially; Vd (volume of distribution) — single value.
  • Two-compartment model — drug distributes initially into central compartment (plasma, well-perfused organs), then into peripheral compartment (fat, muscle); plasma concentration shows biexponential decline (distribution phase + elimination phase).
  • Vc (central compartment volume) — initial volume; Vd(ss) (steady-state Vd); Vd(extrapolated) / Vd(β) — calculated by extrapolating elimination phase to time zero; Vd(ss) preferred.

Clinical Pearl

Vd is a theoretical (apparent) volume — not a real anatomical space. Drugs with low Vd (3–5 L) are confined to plasma — large molecules (heparin), highly protein-bound (warfarin, NSAIDs); drugs with intermediate Vd (10–20 L) distribute in ECF — aminoglycosides, penicillins, lithium; drugs with high Vd (>40 L, may exceed body weight) distribute widely in tissues — digoxin (Vd 500 L), amiodarone (Vd 60 L/kg), tricyclic antidepressants, chloroquine. Vd affects: loading dose calculation (high Vd needs high loading dose), half-life (t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Clearance), dialysability (low Vd + low protein binding = dialysable), and toxicity management. Always check Vd before recommending haemodialysis in overdose — digoxin (Vd 500 L, 25% protein-bound) is NOT removed by dialysis; use Fab antibody. Lithium (Vd ~0.6 L/kg, no protein binding) IS removed by dialysis. Disease states alter Vd — heart failure ↓ Vd (reduced perfusion); uraemia ↑ Vd (↓ protein binding of acidic drugs); cirrhosis ↑ Vd (↓ albumin, ascites); obesity ↑ Vd for lipophilic drugs (amiodarone, diazepam). Always adjust dose in disease — dehydrated patients may need lower dose (↓ Vd → ↑ plasma concentration); overloaded patients may need higher dose (↑ Vd).
