Introduction

Vasodilators are drugs that relax vascular smooth muscle → dilate blood vessels → ↓ peripheral vascular resistance &/or venous return. Used in hypertension, heart failure, angina, pulmonary hypertension, and hypertensive emergencies.

Classification by Site of Action

  • Predominantly arteriolar — Hydralazine, Minoxidil, Diazoxide, Calcium channel blockers (DHP), Fenoldopam.
  • Predominantly venous — Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide).
  • Arteriolar + venous (balanced) — Sodium nitroprusside, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, α1-blockers.

Classification by Mechanism

1. Direct-Acting Vasodilators

  • NO donors / Nitrovasodilators:
    • Nitroglycerin, Isosorbide dinitrate, Isosorbide mononitrate — release NO → activate guanylyl cyclase → ↑cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation; predominantly venous; used for angina, acute heart failure, ACS.
    • Sodium nitroprusside — releases NO spontaneously (non-enzymatic); balanced arteriolar + venous vasodilation; IV for hypertensive emergency, acute heart failure; cyanide & thiocyanate toxicity.
    • Am yl nitrite, sodium nitrite — cyanide poisoning (form methaemoglobin).
  • Potassium channel openers:
    • Minoxidil — opens ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels (KATP) → hyperpolarisation → closes voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → vasodilation; potent arteriolar dilator; used for severe resistant hypertension; topical for alopecia (hair growth — side effect); adverse — reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, hypertrichosis, pericardial effusion.
    • Diazoxide — opens KATP; IV for hypertensive emergency; hyperglycaemia (inhibits insulin release); fluid retention.
    • Nicorandil — nitrate + KATP opener; antianginal.
    • Pinacidil — investigational; hypertension.
  • Hydralazine:
    • Mechanism unclear — likely activates guanylyl cyclase → ↑cGMP; releases NO from endothelium; ↓ Ca²⁺ influx.
    • Arteriolar vasodilator (greater than venous).
    • Uses — hypertension (especially pregnancy — with nitrates for heart failure in African-Americans); severe hypertension; pre-eclampsia.
    • Adverse — reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, headache, flushing, lupus-like syndrome (especially slow acetylators — HLA-DR4), peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine antagonist).
  • Sodium nitroprusside:
    • Releases NO spontaneously (non-enzymatic, no tissue metabolism required).
    • Balanced arteriolar + venous vasodilation; rapid onset (seconds); short duration (1–2 min); IV infusion.
    • Uses — hypertensive emergency, acute heart failure, acute pulmonary oedema, controlled hypotension in surgery.
    • Adverse — hypotension, cyanide & thiocyanate toxicity (especially renal impairment, >48 h use, high dose >4 µg/kg/min); methaemoglobinaemia.
    • Antidote — sodium thiosulfate (cyanide detoxification); hydroxocobalamin.

2. Calcium Channel Blockers (DHP)

  • Amlodipine, Nifedipine, Felodipine, Nicardipine, Lercanidipine, Nitrendipine, Clevidipine.
  • Block L-type Ca²⁺ channels in vascular smooth muscle → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx → vasodilation (arteriolar > venous); minimal effect on heart.
  • Uses — hypertension, angina, Raynaud's, pulmonary hypertension.
  • Adverse — reflex tachycardia (short-acting nifedipine — avoid), flushing, headache, peripheral oedema, gingival hyperplasia.

3. Renin-Angiotensin System Inhibitors

  • ACE inhibitors (ACEIs) — Enalapril, Lisinopril, Ramipril, Perindopril; block conversion of Ang I → Ang II; ↓aldosterone; also block bradykinin degradation → ↑bradykinin (additional vasodilation + cough, angioedema).
  • Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) — Losartan, Valsartan, Telmisartan, Olmesartan; block AT1 receptor; no effect on bradykinin (less cough, angioedema).
  • Direct renin inhibitor — Aliskiren; blocks renin → ↓ Ang I & II; limited use (combination with ACEI/ARB harmful — ONTARGET).
  • ARNI (Sacubitril/Valsartan) — neprilysin inhibitor + ARB; ↑ natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) + block AT1; heart failure.
  • Mechanism — ↓ Ang II → vasodilation (arteriolar + venous); ↓ aldosterone → ↓ Na & water retention; ↓ sympathetic outflow; ↓ vascular remodelling.
  • Uses — hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy, CKD with proteinuria.

4. α-Adrenergic Blockers

  • Non-selective (α1 + α2) — Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible — phaeochromocytoma), Phentolamine (reversible).
  • Selective α1-blockers — Prazosin, Terazosin, Doxazosin, Tamsulosin (uroselective), Silodosin.
  • Mechanism — block α1 on vascular smooth muscle → ↓ Ca²⁺ → vasodilation (arteriolar + venous); also relax prostate & bladder neck smooth muscle.
  • Uses — hypertension (not first-line; doxazosin in ALLHAT showed ↑ heart failure), BPH, phaeochromocytoma (phenoxybenzamine), PTSD (prazosin for nightmares).
  • Adverse — first-dose hypotension (especially postural), syncope, dizziness, palpitations, nasal congestion, ejaculation failure (retrograde).

5. Centrally Acting Sympatholytics

  • Clonidine, Methyldopa, Guanfacine, Guanabenz — α2 agonists in brainstem → ↓ sympathetic outflow → vasodilation.
  • Dexmedetomidine — α2A-selective; IV; ICU sedation.
  • Uses — hypertension (resistant, pregnancy for methyldopa), opioid withdrawal, ADHD, glaucoma (brimonidine).
  • Adverse — sedation, dry mouth, bradycardia, rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal.

  • Fenoldopam — D1 receptor agonist; renal & peripheral vasodilation; IV for hypertensive emergency; preserves renal blood flow.

Introduction

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) — a water-soluble vitamin essential for DNA synthesis (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, methionine synthase), myelination, and erythropoiesis. Deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia, peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord, and cognitive impairment.

Preparations of Vitamin B12

1. Cyanocobalamin

  • Most common pharmaceutical preparation; stable; inexpensive.
  • Cyanide group attached to cobalt — released & detoxified in body (small amount; safe).
  • Routes — oral, sublingual, IM, IV, intranasal (newer — Forte, Nascobal).
  • Requires conversion in body to active forms (methylcobalamin, adenosylcobalamin).
  • Uses — B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, vegan diet, post-gastrectomy, ileal disease); cyanide poisoning (forms cyanocobalamin — excreted; high doses — sodium thiosulfate + hydroxocobalamin preferred).

2. Hydroxocobalamin

  • Preferred in UK & Europe for B12 deficiency (longer retention than cyanocobalamin; less frequent dosing).
  • Hydroxyl group on cobalt.
  • Routes — IM (preferred; well-retained); IV.
  • Converted to active coenzyme forms (methylcobalamin, adenosylcobalamin).
  • Also used for cyanide poisoning — binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) — excreted in urine; preferred over sodium nitrite (does not cause methaemoglobinaemia); dose 5 g IV (Cyanokit); turns skin & urine red (harmless).
  • Adverse — anaphylaxis (rare); acneiform rash; hypotension (rapid IV).

3. Methylcobalamin

  • Active coenzyme form; methyl group on cobalt.
  • Cofactor for methionine synthase — converts homocysteine to methionine; required for DNA synthesis (folate cycle).
  • Routes — oral, sublingual, IM, IV.
  • Available as "active B12" — preferred by some for neurological symptoms (diabetic neuropathy — though evidence limited).
  • Uses — B12 deficiency; diabetic neuropathy (off-label); homocystinuria; psychiatric disorders.

4. Adenosylcobalamin (Dibencozide)

  • Active coenzyme form; 5'-deoxyadenosyl group on cobalt.
  • Cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase — converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA (Krebs cycle); important in fatty acid & amino acid metabolism.
  • Routes — oral, sublingual.
  • Uses — B12 deficiency; athletic performance (unproven); methylmalonic aciduria.

Pharmacological Functions (Physiological Roles)

1. DNA Synthesis — Critical for Erythropoiesis & Cell Division

  1. Methionine synthase (cytoplasm):
    • Cofactor: methylcobalamin.
    • Converts homocysteine → methionine (transfers methyl group from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine).
    • Methionine → S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) — universal methyl donor for DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids, neurotransmitters.
    • Regenerates tetrahydrofolate (THF) from N5-methyl-THF — "folate trap" (without B12, folate is trapped as N5-methyl-THF, unavailable for DNA synthesis).
    • Result — B12 deficiency → folate trap → impaired DNA synthesis → megaloblastic anaemia.
  2. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (mitochondria):
    • Cofactor: adenosylcobalamin.
    • Converts methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (Krebs cycle); important for odd-chain fatty acid & certain amino acid (valine, isoleucine, methionine, threonine) catabolism.
    • Result — B12 deficiency → ↑ methylmalonic acid (MMA) → neurological damage (abnormal fatty acid synthesis in myelin).

2. Myelination & Neurological Function

  • Required for myelin synthesis & maintenance — via methionine/SAM pathway (methylation of myelin basic protein).
  • B12 deficiency → subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord — demyelination of posterior & lateral columns (dorsal columns — loss of proprioception, vibration; lateral corticospinal tracts — weakness, spasticity; spinocerebellar tracts — ataxia).
  • Peripheral neuropathy — symmetric, distal, sensory > motor.
  • Optic neuropathy — visual loss, centrocecal scotoma.
  • Cognitive impairment, dementia, depression, psychosis ("megaloblastic madness").
  • MMA accumulation is neurotoxic; abnormal fatty acid incorporation into myelin.

3. Haematopoiesis

  • Required for normal red blood cell maturation — DNA synthesis; without B12, nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony → megaloblastic anaemia (macrocytic, hypersegmented neutrophils, pancytopenia).
  • Effective erythropoiesis → normal haemoglobin.

4. Homocysteine Metabolism

  • B12 (with folate & B6) metabolises homocysteine.
  • Deficiency → hyperhomocysteinaemia — independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease (atherosclerosis), venous thromboembolism, neural tube defects, cognitive decline.
  • B12 supplementation lowers homocysteine; uncertain CV benefit.

5. Other Functions

  • Conversion of folate to active THF (folate trap mechanism).
  • Synthesis of neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline) — via SAM methylation.
  • Maintenance of bone marrow, GI epithelium, reproductive organs (rapidly dividing cells).
  • Iron metabolism — supports erythropoiesis.

Daily Requirement & Sources

  • RDA — adults 2.4 µg/day; pregnancy 2.6 µg; lactation 2.8 µg.
  • Sources — animal products only (meat, liver, fish, eggs, dairy); not in plants (vegans at risk).
  • Body stores — 2–5 mg (in liver); sufficient for 3–5 years without dietary intake (reason why deficiency takes years to develop).

Absorption

  1. B12 released from food protein by gastric acid & pepsin.
  2. Binds to R-protein (haptocorrin) from saliva & gastric juice (high affinity at acidic pH).
  3. In duodenum, pancreatic enzymes degrade R-protein; B12 binds to intrinsic factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells.
  4. B12-IF complex travels to terminal ileum; binds to cubilin receptor on ileal enterocytes; absorbed by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  5. In blood, B12 binds to transcobalamin II (active transport to tissues) & haptocorrin (transcobalamin I) (storage).

Causes of Deficiency

  • Pernicious anaemia — autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells → ↓ IF; anti-parietal cell & anti-IF antibodies.
  • Gastrectomy / bariatric surgery — loss of parietal cells & IF.
  • Terminal ileal disease — Crohn's, resection, coeliac, tropical sprue, blind loop (bacterial overgrowth consumes B12), Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm).
  • Dietary — strict vegan; breastfed infants of vegan mothers.
  • Atrophic gastritis (elderly) — ↓ acid → ↓ B12 release from protein.
  • Proton pump inhibitors (long-term) — ↓ acid → ↓ B12 release; controversial.
  • Metformin (long-term) — ↓ B12 absorption (calcium-dependent IF-receptor interaction).
  • Nitrous oxide abuse — oxidises cobalt (Co⁺ → Co²⁺) → inactivates B12.
  • Congenital — Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome (cubilin defect); transcobalamin II deficiency.

Treatment

  • Pernicious anaemia / malabsorption — IM hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg on alternate days for 2 weeks (or until symptoms improve), then 1000 µg every 1–3 months lifelong.
  • Dietary deficiency (no malabsorption) — oral cyanocobalamin 1000–2000 µg daily; or IM 1000 µg monthly.
  • High-dose oral (1000 µg/day) — effective even in pernicious anaemia (1% passive absorption when dose high); convenient; emerging alternative to IM.
  • Sublingual — effective; convenient.
  • Intranasal — Nascobal 500 µg weekly; convenient for maintenance.
  • Severe deficiency (neurological symptoms) — IM 1000 µg every other day for 2 weeks (or until symptoms stop improving); then monthly.
  • Cyanide poisoning — IV hydroxocobalamin 5 g (Cyanokit).

Adverse Effects

  • Generally safe; water-soluble; excess excreted in urine.
  • Allergic reactions (rare) — anaphylaxis, especially with parenteral.
  • Hypokalaemia (severe deficiency treatment — due to rapid erythropoiesis taking up K⁺); monitor & replace.
  • Acneiform rash.
  • Red discolouration of urine (hydroxocobalamin — cyanide poisoning).
  • Counterfeit B12 ("shotgun" vitamin cocktails) — risk of unnecessary injections.

Clinical Pearl

B12 deficiency should be suspected in: macrocytic anaemia (MCV >100), hypersegmented neutrophils, pancytopenia, peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (loss of vibration & proprioception, weakness), cognitive decline, glossitis, infertility. Always check B12 in elderly, vegans, post-gastrectomy, metformin users, nitrous oxide abusers. Diagnosis — low serum B12 (<200 pg/mL); if borderline (200–400), check methylmalonic acid (MMA) & homocysteine (both elevated in B12 deficiency); normal in folate deficiency (only homocysteine elevated). Anti-parietal cell & anti-IF antibodies — pernicious anaemia. Distinguish B12 vs folate deficiency — both cause megaloblastic anaemia; B12 deficiency causes neurological symptoms (posterior column, lateral column, peripheral neuropathy); folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological symptoms; ALWAYS exclude B12 deficiency before treating with folate alone — folate will correct anaemia but allow neurological damage to progress (irreversible). IM hydroxocobalamin is preferred for pernicious anaemia & severe deficiency (longer retention, less frequent dosing); 1000 µg on alternate days for 2 weeks, then monthly. High-dose oral cyanocobalamin (1000–2000 µg/day) — effective even in pernicious anaemia (1% passive absorption); convenient; emerging alternative. Watch for hypokalaemia in severe deficiency treatment — rapid erythropoiesis takes up K⁺; monitor & replace. Hydroxocobalamin IV 5 g (Cyanokit) is antidote for cyanide poisoning — binds cyanide → cyanocobalamin (B12) → excreted in urine; preferred over sodium nitrite (does not cause methaemoglobinaemia); turns skin & urine red (harmless). India — B12 deficiency common (vegetarian diet, pernicious anaemia); cheap cyanocobalamin widely available; metformin users (diabetes) — monitor.

Introduction

Low Molecular Weight Heparins (LMWHs) are derived from unfractionated heparin (UFH) by chemical or enzymatic depolymerisation. They have average molecular weight 4,000–6,500 Da (vs UFH 15,000 Da). LMWHs have largely replaced UFH for many indications due to predictable pharmacokinetics, better safety profile, and convenient SC administration without routine monitoring.

Examples

  • Enoxaparin — most widely used; 40 mg = 4000 IU anti-Xa.
  • Dalteparin — 2500–18,000 IU.
  • Tinzaparin — 50 IU/kg (therapeutic) or 4500 IU (prophylactic).
  • Nadroparin.
  • Reviparin.
  • Parnaparin.
  • Bemiparin — second-generation; lowest MW; longest half-life.

Mechanism of Action

  1. LMWH binds to antithrombin III (AT) via a specific pentasaccharide sequence — same as UFH.
  2. Binding induces conformational change in AT → accelerates AT-mediated inactivation of clotting factors.
  3. Key difference from UFH:
    • UFH (long chain ≥18 saccharides) — inhibits both thrombin (IIa) & factor Xa equally (1:1 ratio).
    • LMWH (short chain, <18 saccharides) — preferentially inhibits factor Xa (ratio 2:1 to 4:1 anti-Xa : anti-IIa); shorter chain cannot simultaneously bind thrombin & AT.
    • Fondaparinux (pure pentasaccharide) — exclusively inhibits factor Xa (100% anti-Xa, 0% anti-IIa).
  4. ↓ Factor Xa → ↓ thrombin generation → ↓ fibrin formation → anticoagulation.

Pharmacokinetics (Advantages over UFH)

  • SC bioavailability — ~90–100% (vs UFH 30%); predictable absorption.
  • Onset — 3–5 h after SC.
  • Half-life — 4–6 h (vs UFH 1–2 h); allows once or twice daily dosing.
  • Metabolism — hepatic desulphation & depolymerisation; partial renal excretion (40%).
  • Renal excretion — more than UFH; caution in renal impairment (CrCl <30); dose reduction or avoid; UFH preferred in severe CKD.
  • Less binding to plasma proteins, endothelial cells, macrophages — more predictable pharmacokinetics; less variability.
  • Less binding to osteoclasts — ↓ risk of osteoporosis.
  • Less binding to platelet factor 4 (PF4) — ↓ risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
  • Does not significantly prolong aPTT — routine aPTT monitoring NOT required (predictable dose-response); monitor anti-Xa level if needed (pregnancy, obesity, renal impairment, children).
  • Does not cross placenta — safe in pregnancy (preferred over warfarin).

Therapeutic Uses

  1. VTE prophylaxis (high-risk patients):
    • Medical inpatients (immobile, elderly).
    • Surgical patients (orthopaedic — hip/knee replacement; abdominal, pelvic, cancer surgery).
    • Acute stroke with immobility.
    • Critical care.
    • Dose — enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily; dalteparin 5000 IU SC daily.
  2. VTE treatment (DVT & PE):
    • Acute & long-term; bridge to warfarin/DOAC.
    • Cancer-associated thrombosis (CAT) — LMWH preferred for 3–6 months (CLOT trial); reduces recurrence vs warfarin.
    • Pregnancy-associated VTE — preferred; dose adjusted by weight (or anti-Xa monitoring).
    • Dose — enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC every 12 h OR 1.5 mg/kg SC once daily; dalteparin 200 IU/kg daily; tinzaparin 175 IU/kg daily.
  3. Acute coronary syndrome (ACS):
    • Unstable angina / NSTEMI — enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC every 12 h (with aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor); preferred over UFH in conservatively-managed patients.
    • STEMI — with fibrinolysis (ExTRACT-TIMI 25 trial — enoxaparin superior to UFH; age >75: 0.75 mg/kg every 12 h; CrCl <30: 1 mg/kg daily).
    • STEMI with primary PCI — UFH or bivalirudin preferred (catheter thrombosis risk with LMWH).
  4. Haemodialysis / extracorporeal circuits — anticoagulation of dialysis circuit.
  5. Mechanical heart valves (pregnancy) — preferred over warfarin.
  6. Antiphospholipid syndrome (pregnancy) — with low-dose aspirin.
  7. Atrial fibrillation (perioperative bridging) — when warfarin held for surgery.
  8. Superficial vein thrombosis — fondaparinux preferred; LMWH alternative.
  9. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

Modern pharmacology combines natural, synthetic, & biotechnological sources. Introduction

When two or more drugs are administered together, their combined effect may be greater than, less than, or equal to the sum of their individual effects. These interactions are classified as synergism (greater) or antagonism (less).

Drug Synergism

Definition — combined effect of two drugs is greater than the sum of their individual effects (1 + 1 > 2).

Types

  1. Additive (summation):
    • Combined effect = sum of individual effects (1 + 1 = 2).
    • Drugs act by same or different mechanisms but produce same end effect.
    • Examples:
      • Aspirin + paracetamol — analgesia.
      • Sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim (co-trimoxazole) — antibacterial (sequential blockade of folate pathway).
      • Amoxicillin + clavulanic acid — antibacterial (β-lactamase inhibition).
      • Hydralazine + hydrochlorothiazide — antihypertensive.
      • ACEI + thiazide — antihypertensive.
      • Two NMBDs (neuromuscular blockers).
  2. Supra-additive (potentiation):
    • Combined effect > sum of individual effects (1 + 1 > 2).
    • One drug enhances the effect of another.
    • Examples:
      • Acetylcholine + physostigmine — physostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase → ↑ acetylcholine → potentiation.
      • Adrenaline + cocaine — cocaine blocks noradrenaline reuptake → ↑ adrenaline effect.
      • Levodopa + carbidopa — carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase → ↑ levodopa delivery to brain; ↑ effect; ↓ peripheral side effects.
      • 5-Fluorouracil + leucovorin — leucovorin enhances 5-FU binding to thymidylate synthase → ↑ anticancer effect.
      • Sulbactam + ampicillin, clavulanate + amoxicillin, tazobactam + piperacillin — β-lactamase inhibitor protects β-lactam.
      • Penicillin + probenecid — probenecid blocks penicillin renal excretion → ↑ penicillin levels.
      • Trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole — sequential blockade of bacterial folate synthesis.
      • Amphotericin B + flucytosine — amphotericin increases flucytosine entry into fungal cell.
      • ACEI + thiazide — thiazide activates RAAS which ACEI blocks → enhanced antihypertensive effect.
      • β-lactam + aminoglycoside — cell wall damage by β-lactam enhances aminoglycoside entry.

Drug Antagonism

Definition — combined effect of two drugs is less than the sum of their individual effects (1 + 1 < 2); one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another.

Types

  1. Pharmaceutical (incompatibility):
    • Chemical or physical reaction before administration.
    • Examples — protamine + heparin (neutralisation); chelating agents + heavy metals; tetracycline + dairy/Ca/Mg/Fe; penicillin + aminoglycoside in same IV line.
  2. Pharmacokinetic:
    • One drug alters absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion of another.
    • Examples — enzyme inducers (rifampin, phenytoin ↓ warfarin, OCP); enzyme inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole ↑ warfarin, statins); antacids ↓ ketoconazole; probenecid ↓ penicillin excretion (paradoxical synergy for syphilis).
  3. Pharmacodynamic:
    • Both drugs act on same or different receptors/systems with opposite effects.
    • Competitive (surmountable) — naloxone + morphine; atropine + acetylcholine; propranolol + adrenaline.
    • Non-competitive (insurmountable) — phenoxybenzamine + adrenaline; aspirin + COX.
    • Physiological (functional) — histamine vs adrenaline; insulin vs glucagon; ACh vs adrenaline on heart.
    • Chemical — protamine + heparin; deferoxamine + iron; digoxin Fab + digoxin.

Clinical Significance

  • Therapeutic synergy — antibiotic combinations (co-trimoxazole, amoxicillin-clavulanate); antihypertensive combinations (ACEI + thiazide); cancer chemotherapy combinations; tuberculosis (HRZE — prevents resistance).
  • Antidotes (antagonism) — naloxone (opioid); flumazenil (benzodiazepine); atropine + pralidoxime (OPC); protamine (heparin); vitamin K (warfarin); deferoxamine (iron); idarucizumab (dabigatran).
  • Adverse interactions — warfarin + rifampin (↓ anticoagulation); OCP + rifampin (contraceptive failure); statin + macrolide (↑ rhabdomyolysis); SSRI + MAOI (serotonin syndrome); β-blocker + verapamil (bradycardia, AV block).

Clinical Pearl

Synergism is exploited in combination therapy — co-trimoxazole (sequential folate blockade), amoxicillin-clavulanate (β-lactamase protection), levodopa-carbidopa (peripheral decarboxylase inhibition), HRZE for TB (prevents resistance & enhances efficacy). Antagonism is exploited in antidotes — naloxone for opioid overdose, atropine + pralidoxime for organophosphate poisoning, flumazenil for benzodiazepine overdose, protamine for heparin. Always check drug interactions before prescribing — warfarin has >100 interactions; monitor INR; rifampin (potent inducer) reduces warfarin, OCP, tacrolimus; macrolides + statins cause rhabdomyolysis; SSRI + MAOI = serotonin syndrome (life-threatening). Pharmacodynamic antagonism is the basis for many therapeutic strategies — β-blocker blocks adrenaline effect (hypertension, angina); ACEI blocks angiotensin II (hypertension, HF); antihistamine blocks histamine (allergy); PPI blocks acid (GERD, PUD).

Definition

Fixed Dose Combination (FDC) — a pharmaceutical preparation containing two or more active drugs in a fixed ratio of doses, in a single dosage form (tablet, capsule, injection) administered together.

Rationale

  1. Synergistic / additive therapeutic effect — combined effect > sum; lower doses of each drug achieve same effect with fewer side effects.
  2. Counteract adverse effects — one drug offsets side effect of another (e.g., levodopa + carbidopa; isoniazid + pyridoxine).
  3. Simplified regimen — single pill vs multiple pills; improves adherence (especially chronic diseases — HIV, TB, hypertension, diabetes).
  4. Prevent resistance — multiple drugs attack different targets; reduces chance of resistance (TB, HIV, malaria).
  5. Cost reduction — FDC often cheaper than separate components.
  6. Target multiple pathophysiological mechanisms — hypertension (ACEI + CCB); diabetes (metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor); COPD (LABA + ICS + LAMA).

Advantages of FDCs

  • Improved adherence — fewer pills; convenient; especially for chronic diseases.
  • Synergistic effect — enhanced efficacy; lower doses of individual components; fewer side effects.
  • Counteract side effects — one drug offsets adverse effect of another (carbidopa prevents levodopa peripheral side effects; isoniazid + pyridoxine prevents neuropathy).
  • Prevent resistance — multiple drugs (TB, HIV, malaria, antibiotics).
  • Cost-effective — single pill often cheaper; reduced hospitalisation from better control.
  • Simplified prescribing & dispensing.
  • Multiple pathophysiological mechanisms — comprehensive disease control.
  • Improved outcomes — better BP control, glycemic control, viral suppression.

Disadvantages & Concerns

  • Fixed dose ratio — cannot titrate individual components; inflexible dosing.
  • Toxicity of one drug requires stopping all — e.g., rifampicin hepatotoxicity means stopping whole TB FDC; need separate drugs to continue.
  • Adverse reaction identification — difficult to identify which component caused side effect.
  • Pharmacokinetic mismatch — different half-lives; one component may accumulate; formulation challenge (e.g., rifampicin degrades in presence of isoniazid — stabilised with barrier).
  • Bioequivalence — FDC must be bioequivalent to separate components; not always tested.
  • Cost — some FDCs more expensive than individual generics.
  • Irrational FDCs — many irrational combinations marketed (especially in India) without scientific basis; e.g., antibiotics + antipyretics + antihistamines; NSAID combinations; cough-cold combinations with multiple ingredients.
  • Promotes antibiotic resistance — irrational antibiotic FDCs (amoxicillin + cefixime, etc.) — fixed doses; inappropriate use; broad-spectrum overuse.
  • Difficulty in dose adjustment — in renal/hepatic impairment, elderly, children; may need separate components.
  • Regulatory concern — many FDCs approved without adequate safety/efficacy data; banned by regulators (India banned 344 FDCs in 2016).

Criteria for Rational FDC

  1. Components should have:
    • Same indication / disease target.
    • Complementary mechanism of action.
    • Similar pharmacokinetics (half-life, dosing frequency).
    • Evidence of additive/synergistic effect.
    • Reduced side effect of one by another, or lower doses achieved.
    • Improved adherence.
  3. Should be more effective or safer than individual components alone.
  4. Cost-effective.
  5. Quality, safety, efficacy established by clinical trials.
  6. Approved by regulatory authority.

Irrational FDCs (Common in India)

  • Antibiotic + antipyretic + antihistamine (amoxicillin + paracetamol + phenylephrine + chlorpheniramine — for "cold").
  • Multiple NSAIDs together (ibuprofen + paracetamol + nimesulide).
  • Antacid + anti-ulcer + enzyme mixtures.
  • Cough mixtures with 4+ ingredients (dextromethorphan + chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine + paracetamol + caffeine + guaiphenesin + ammonium chloride).
  • Two antibiotics from same class (amoxicillin + cefixime — both β-lactams; irrational).
  • Ranitidine + domperidone + enzymes (anti-ulcer, no rationale).
  • NSAID + muscle relaxant + antacid (some useful, many irrational).
  • Multivitamin + mineral + antioxidant cocktails (no proven benefit).

India's FDC Regulation

  • CDSCO ban March 2016 — banned 344 irrational FDCs (including combinations like Nimesulide + Paracetamol, Amoxicillin + Cefixime, Ondansetron + Paracetamol, etc.); based on Chandrasekharan committee report.
  • Subsequent litigation — some bans overturned by Delhi High Court; Supreme Court upheld ban for most in 2019.
  • Continued monitoring — ban on additional FDCs in 2018, 2019, 2023.
  • WHO & ICMR guidelines — rational use of FDCs; specifically ban irrational antibiotic combinations.

Clinical Pearl

FDCs are rational when components have complementary mechanisms, similar pharmacokinetics, evidence of synergy, & improved outcomes — e.g., co-trimoxazole, HRZE for TB, ART single-tablet regimens, ACEI + CCB for hypertension, ICS + LABA for asthma. Avoid irrational FDCs — antibiotic + antipyretic + antihistamine combinations; multiple NSAIDs; broad-spectrum antibiotic combinations (amoxicillin + cefixime); complex cough mixtures with no clear rationale. India banned 344 irrational FDCs in 2016 (Nimesulide + Paracetamol, Amoxicillin + Cefixime, Ondansetron + Paracetamol); Supreme Court upheld ban in 2019; additional bans in 2018, 2019, 2023. Always prefer single-drug formulations when possible — allows titration; identifies side effects; cheaper. FDCs are useful for: chronic diseases (TB, HIV, hypertension, diabetes, asthma) — improve adherence; multi-target therapy (H. pylori, malaria ACT); preventing resistance. When toxicity develops, may need to switch to separate components — e.g., rifampicin hepatotoxicity in TB FDC — need to stop all & reintroduce individually. Patient education — FDC means multiple drugs in one pill; do not take additional separate components (risk of overdose); check labels.

Definition

Drug allergy is an immunologically mediated adverse drug reaction — the drug or its metabolite acts as an antigen (hapten) and triggers a specific immune response (Type I–IV hypersensitivity). Distinguishes from non-immunological adverse reactions (side effects, toxicity, idiosyncratic).

Drug allergies account for ~5–10% of all adverse drug reactions; most are mild but some are life-threatening (anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN).

Pathogenesis

Most drugs are small molecules (<1000 Da) — not immunogenic alone; act as haptens — bind to host proteins → form complete antigen → trigger immune response.

  • Drug (hapten) + host protein (carrier) → antigen → antigen-presenting cells → T cell activation → humoral (B cell, antibody) or cellular (T cell) response.
  • Some drugs bind directly to immune receptors (e.g., β-lactams to TCR; non-hapten mechanism — p-i concept — pharmacological interaction with immune receptors).
  • Drug-specific IgE, IgG, IgM antibodies; T cell-mediated responses (Type IV); immune complexes.

Gell & Coombs Classification

Type I — Immediate (IgE-mediated) — Minutes to 1 hour

  • Mechanism — drug-specific IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells & basophils; re-exposure → allergen cross-links IgE → degranulation → histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, PAF.
  • Clinical — urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, GI cramps, anaphylaxis (life-threatening).
  • Drugs — β-lactam antibiotics (penicillin — classic); cephalosporins (less common); sulphonamides; NSAIDs (aspirin — pseudo-allergic, non-IgE); muscle relaxants (suxamethonium, vecuronium); insulin; latex; chemotherapy (platinum — cisplatin); monoclonal antibodies (infliximab, rituximab).
  • Tests — skin prick test (immediate wheal & flare); serum specific IgE (RAST); basophil activation test; serum tryptase (anaphylaxis); drug challenge (cautious, specialist).
  • Treatment — antihistamines (H1 ± H2); corticosteroids; adrenaline IM (anaphylaxis); bronchodilators; oxygen; IV fluids.

Type II — Cytotoxic (IgG/IgM-mediated) — Hours to days

  • Mechanism — IgG/IgM antibodies bind drug-modified cells → complement activation or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) → cell lysis.
  • Clinical — haemolytic anaemia (penicillin, cephalosporin, methyldopa — autoantibody; quinine, quinidine — hapten); thrombocytopenia (heparin — HIT; quinine, sulfonamides, vancomycin); neutropenia (clozapine, antithyroid, sulfasalazine); agranulocytosis.
  • Drugs — penicillins, cephalosporins, methyldopa, quinine, quinidine, heparin, NSAIDs, antithyroid drugs.
  • Tests — direct antiglobulin test (DAT); indirect Coombs; antibody detection; platelet factor 4 (PF4) antibody (HIT).
  • Treatment — stop drug; corticosteroids; IVIG; transfusion (severe); plasmapheresis.

Type III — Immune complex (IgG/IgM) — 1–3 weeks

  • Mechanism — antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissues (kidney, skin, joints, vessels) → complement activation → neutrophil chemotaxis → tissue damage.
  • Clinical — serum sickness (fever, urticaria, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, proteinuria, vasculitis); Arthus reaction (local immune complex); drug-induced lupus erythematosus; vasculitis.
  • Drugs — antitoxins (horse serum — tetanus, diphtheria, snake antivenom); penicillin, sulfonamides; thiazides; hydralazine, procainamide (drug-induced lupus); minocycline; anti-TNF biologics (paradoxical).
  • Tests — complement levels (C3, C4 — low); immune complex assays; biopsy (tissue immunofluorescence).
  • Treatment — stop drug; corticosteroids; antihistamines; NSAIDs; plasmapheresis (severe).

Type IV — Delayed (T-cell-mediated) — 2–7 days

Sub-classified (Gell-Coombs revised):

  • Type IVa — Th1-mediated — MAC (maculopapular exanthem); contact dermatitis; tuberculin reaction.
  • Type IVb — Th2-mediated — DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms); maculopapular exanthem with eosinophilia.
  • Type IVc — Cytotoxic T cell (CD8+) — SJS/TEN (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis); AGEP (Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis); hepatitis.
  • Type IVd — Th17-mediated — AGEP; pustular psoriasis-like.
  • Drugs:
    • SJS/TEN — allopurinol, sulfonamides, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine), nevirapine, NSAIDs (oxicam), antimalarials; HLA-B*15:02 (carbamazepine — Han Chinese); HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol).

  • Previous allergic reaction to same or related drug.
  • Atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema) — risk of severe IgE-mediated reactions.
  • HLA associations — HLA-B*15:02 (carbamazepine in Han Chinese, Thai, Indian — test before starting); HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol — Han Chinese, Thai, Korean); HLA-B*57:01 (abacavir — all populations, must test before starting); HLA-A*31:01 (carbamazepine — Europeans, Japanese); HLA-B*35:02 (dapsone); HLA-DQA1*05:01 (lacosamide).

  • Age — adults more than children; elderly more severe reactions.
  • Female sex — slightly higher.

  • Parenteral (IV/IM) route — higher risk than oral.

  • Viral infections (EBV — ampicillin rash; HIV — sulfonamide; HIV — abacavir).

  1. Detailed history:
    • Drug name, dose, route, dates of administration & reaction onset.
    • Symptoms — rash (describe morphology, distribution, progression), itching, fever, mucosal involvement, breathing difficulty, hypotension, joint pain.
    • Timing — immediate (minutes — IgE Type I); delayed (days-weeks — Type IV).
    • Previous exposure & reactions.
    • Concurrent illnesses, viral infection (EBV, HIV).
    • Atopy, family history of allergy.
  2. Examination:
    • Vital signs — anaphylaxis (hypotension, bronchospasm, tachycardia).
    • Skin — morphology (urticaria, maculopapular, target, bullous, pustular, erythroderma); mucosa; BSA involved (SJS/TEN); Nikolsky sign.
    • Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly (DRESS).
    • Systemic — lungs, heart.
  3. Investigations:
    • CBG — eosinophilia (Type IVb); atypical lymphocytes (DRESS).
    • LFT — hepatitis (DRESS, SJS/TEN, drug-induced).
    • Renal — interstitial nephritis.
    • Serum tryptase — elevated within 1–4 h of anaphylaxis; baseline (mast cell load); confirms mast cell activation.
    • Complement — C3, C4 (low in Type III).
    • Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) — haemolytic anaemia (Type II).
    • Skin biopsy — histology for SJS/TEN (epidermal necrosis), DRESS, AGEP.
    • HHV-6 serology/PCR — DRESS.
    • Skin tests — prick, intradermal, patch.
    • Specific IgE (RAST) — penicillin, latex, insulin, muscle relaxants.
    • Basophil activation test (CD63/CD203c).
    • HLA typing — before high-risk drugs (HLA-B*15:02 carbamazepine; HLA-B*57:01 abacavir; HLA-B*58:01 allopurinol).
    • Lymphocyte transformation test (LTT) — research.
    • Drug provocation test — last resort; specialist; risk-benefit; for essential drug with no alternative.

Management

1. Stop the Drug

  • Most important step.
  • Avoid for life if severe reaction (SJS/TEN, DRESS, anaphylaxis).
  • Document in medical records; medical alert bracelet.

2. Specific Treatment

3. Desensitisation

  • Indicated when no alternative drug available & treatment essential (e.g., penicillin for neurosyphilis in pregnancy; sulfonamide in Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV; aspirin in CAD with aspirin allergy; chemotherapy; insulin allergy).
  • Gradually increasing doses over hours-days → "tolerance" (not true cure — temporary; wanes if drug stopped).
  • Mechanism — mast cell desensitisation; IgE internalisation; Treg induction.
  • Specialist; ICU setting; emergency equipment.

  • Avoid unnecessary drugs; rational prescribing.
  • HLA testing before high-risk drugs — HLA-B*15:02 (carbamazepine in Asian); HLA-B*57:01 (abacavir); HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol in Asian).
  • Oral route preferred over parenteral.
  • Antibiotic stewardship — reduce broad-spectrum use.
  • Cross-reactivity awareness — penicillins & cephalosporins (10–15%); sulfonamides; NSAIDs (non-selective).
  • Premedication for radiocontrast (antihistamine + corticosteroid).
  • Medical alert bracelet; patient education.

Definition

Non-maleficence — from Latin primum non nocere ("first, do no harm") — is the ethical principle that healthcare professionals must avoid causing harm to patients, whether through acts of commission (doing something harmful) or omission (failing to do something beneficial). It is one of the four fundamental principles of biomedical ethics (Beauchamp & Childress) — autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice.

Core Concept

Non-maleficence obliges the physician to:

  1. Not inflict harm or evil intentionally.
  2. Not inflict harm through negligence — provide standard of care; act within competence; refer when needed.
  3. Weigh benefits vs risks of every intervention — only proceed if benefits outweigh harms.
  4. Choose the lesser harm when no beneficial option exists.
  5. Prevent harm — anticipate & prevent potential harm (e.g., vaccination, fall precautions, infection control).
  6. Remove harm — remove harmful interventions (e.g., stop nephrotoxic drug in AKI).

Relation to Other Principles

  • Beneficence — positive duty to do good; non-maleficence is negative duty to avoid harm. Often in tension — most interventions carry some risk; balance benefit vs harm.
  • Autonomy — respect patient's right to choose; competent patient may refuse beneficial treatment (autonomy overrides beneficence/non-maleficence in competent adults).
  • Justice — fair distribution of benefits & burdens; avoid discrimination.

Application in Patient Care

1. Medication Safety

  • Prescribe only when indicated; avoid unnecessary polypharmacy.
  • Check for drug interactions, allergies, contraindications, dose adjustments (renal, hepatic, elderly, paediatric, pregnancy).
  • Use correct dose, route, frequency; verify "five rights" — right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time.
  • Monitor for adverse effects; therapeutic drug monitoring (digoxin, lithium, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, anti-epileptics).
  • High-alert medications — anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, chemotherapy, neuromuscular blockers, concentrated electrolytes (KCl), sedatives; double-check; independent verification; protocols.
  • Avoid abbreviations — "U" for units (mistaken for 0); "QD" vs "QID"; "MS" (morphine sulphate vs magnesium sulphate).
  • Legible prescriptions; electronic prescribing; tall man lettering (predniSONE vs prednisoLONE; HYDROmorphone vs morphine).

2. Procedures & Surgery

  • Indicated procedure; competence to perform; informed consent (risks, benefits, alternatives); sterile technique; time-out before procedure; correct site marking.
  • WHO Surgical Safety Checklist — sign in (before anaesthesia), time out (before incision), sign out (before patient leaves OR).
  • Prevent surgical site infection — prophylactic antibiotics within 60 min of incision; normothermia; glycaemic control; hair clipping not shaving.
  • Prevent venous thromboembolism — risk stratification; LMWH; mechanical prophylaxis; early mobilisation.
  • Avoid wrong site, wrong patient, wrong procedure — universal protocol; mark site; verify patient identity.

3. Diagnostic Tests

  • Order only indicated tests; avoid unnecessary radiation (CT); avoid unnecessary blood draws (anaemia in ICU).
  • Consider patient comfort & risk — invasive tests (biopsy, angiography) only when benefits justify.
  • Communicate results promptly; act on critical values.

4. Communication

  • Honest, clear communication — don't deceive, don't give false hope.
  • Break bad news sensitively (SPIKES protocol).
  • Apologise for errors — open disclosure; transparency.
  • Don't abandon patient — continue care even if cure not possible; palliative care.

5. End-of-Life Care

  • Withhold/withdraw futile treatment — life-sustaining treatment that doesn't benefit (vegetative state, terminal illness).
  • Pain & symptom relief — adequate analgesia; double effect — high-dose opioids for pain may hasten death (intended: pain relief; foreseen but unintended: respiratory depression); ethically acceptable if intention is pain relief.
  • Palliative sedation — for refractory symptoms in terminal illness.
  • Advance directives — respect patient's prior wishes; living will; durable power of attorney.
  • Do not resuscitate (DNR) orders — appropriate in terminal illness; discuss with patient & family.
  • Avoid active euthanasia & physician-assisted suicide (illegal in India; ethical debate worldwide).

6. Confidentiality & Privacy

  • Maintain patient confidentiality — except when disclosure is required by law (notifiable diseases, child abuse, court order, danger to self/others).
  • HIPAA-style privacy; secure medical records; minimise unnecessary access.

7. Infection Control

  • Hand hygiene (WHO 5 Moments); aseptic technique; isolation precautions (standard, contact, droplet, airborne); vaccination of HCWs; sharps safety; post-exposure prophylaxis.

8. Patient Safety

  • Prevent falls — risk assessment, bed rails, call bell, non-slip footwear.
  • Prevent pressure ulcers — repositioning, pressure-relieving mattresses, nutrition.
  • Prevent aspiration — head elevation, swallowing assessment, NPO before procedures.
  • Prevent venous thromboembolism — risk stratification, prophylaxis.
  • Prevent catheter-associated infections — aseptic insertion, minimise dwell, closed drainage.
  • Identify patient correctly — two identifiers (name, DOB, hospital number); wristband.

9. Conflict of Interest

  • Declare financial & non-financial conflicts.
  • Avoid self-referral; avoid unnecessary referrals/treatments for financial gain.
  • Pharmaceutical industry interactions — avoid gifts, samples that influence prescribing; generic prescribing.

10. Medical Errors & Disclosure

  • Acknowledge errors — be honest with patient & family; apologise; explain what happened, what will be done to prevent recurrence.
  • Open disclosure — ethical & legal obligation; improves trust; reduces litigation.
  • Root cause analysis — system improvement; just culture (distinguish human error, at-risk behaviour, reckless behaviour).
  • Report to authorities — mandatory for certain errors (wrong site surgery, retained foreign body, sentinel events).

Ethical Tensions

1. Beneficence vs Non-maleficence

  • Most medical interventions have potential harm (surgery, chemotherapy, antibiotics).
  • Balance — only proceed if benefits outweigh harms; minimise harm (use lowest effective dose; least invasive procedure).
  • Example — chemotherapy (toxic but potentially life-saving) — ethical if benefits outweigh toxicity.

2. Autonomy vs Non-maleficence

  • Competent patient may refuse beneficial treatment (blood transfusion in Jehovah's Witness) — autonomy overrides non-maleficence.
  • Incompetent patient (unconscious, dementia, child) — act in best interest; emergency exception.
  • Public health — isolate infectious patient (TB) — restricts autonomy but protects others.

3. Justice vs Non-maleficence

  • Resource allocation — withhold expensive treatment from one patient to provide to many (rationing; utilitarian).
  • Cost of care — expensive drugs may cause financial harm (bankruptcy); ethical prescribing considers cost.

4. Double Effect

  • Action has both good & bad effects.
  • Ethically acceptable if:
    • Action itself is good or neutral.
    • Intention is the good effect (not the bad).
    • Bad effect is not means to good effect.
    • Good effect outweighs bad effect.
  • Example — high-dose opioids for terminal cancer pain (good: pain relief; bad: respiratory depression); ethically acceptable.

Indian Context — Medical Ethics

  • Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002 — code of ethics for Indian physicians; non-maleficence implicit.
  • National Medical Commission (NMC, 2019) — replaced MCI; ethics emphasis.
  • Consumer Protection Act — medical services covered; patients can sue for negligence; courts apply Bolam test (reasonable standard of care) + Bolitho (logical opinion).
  • Criminal negligence (Section 304A IPC) — rash or negligent act causing death; rare but increasing; Supreme Court Jacob Mathew vs State of Punjab (2005) — higher threshold for criminal liability of doctors.
  • MTP Act — termination of pregnancy only within legal framework.
  • PCPNDT Act — prohibition of sex determination.
  • Transplantation of Human Organs Act — organ donation rules.
  • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 — rights of mentally ill; advance directive.
  • HIV & AIDS (Prevention & Control) Act, 2017 — anti-discrimination; confidentiality.
  • Patient Rights Charter — National Human Rights Commission (2018); 17 rights including right to information, confidentiality, second opinion, refuse treatment, safety, redressal.

Clinical Pearl

Non-maleficence — "first, do no harm" — is the most fundamental ethical principle in medicine. It requires balancing benefits against harms of every intervention; competence to practice within limits; recognising & disclosing errors; preventing harm through protocols (hand hygiene, WHO surgical safety checklist, medication safety). The double effect allows interventions with foreseeable harm if the intention is good (e.g., high-dose opioids for terminal pain; chemotherapy for cancer). Always respect competent patient's refusal — autonomy overrides non-maleficence in competent adults (e.g., Jehovah's Witness refusing blood transfusion). Open disclosure of errors — ethical & legal obligation; apologise; explain; improve systems; reduces litigation. Medication safety — verify "five rights"; check interactions, allergies, dose adjustments; high-alert medications (anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, chemotherapy); electronic prescribing; tall man lettering. India — medical negligence litigation increasing; courts apply Bolam test (standard of care expected of a reasonably competent practitioner) + Bolitho (logical basis for opinion); Supreme Court Jacob Mathew (2005) — higher threshold for criminal liability of doctors; Consumer Protection Act covers medical services. Patient safety is non-negotiable — implement WHO surgical safety checklist; infection control bundles; medication reconciliation; falls risk assessment; pressure ulcer prevention; DVT prophylaxis. Always prioritise patient welfare over financial gain — avoid unnecessary tests, procedures, prescriptions; declare conflicts of interest; generic prescribing; rational antibiotic use; antimicrobial stewardship.

Introduction

HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) are the most effective lipid-lowering drugs; cornerstone of cardiovascular disease prevention. They inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, reducing hepatic cholesterol & upregulating LDL receptors.

Classification

  • Natural / Fungal-derived:
    • Lovastatin — first statin (from Aspergillus terreus); US 1987.
    • Simvastatin — semi-synthetic from lovastatin; prodrug.
    • Pravastatin — derived from Penicillium; hydrophilic; non-enzymatic metabolism.
  • Synthetic:
    • Fluvastatin — first fully synthetic.
    • Atorvastatin — most potent; most widely used.
    • Rosuvastatin — most potent; longest half-life.
    • Pitavastatin — newer; minimal CYP metabolism.
  • By potency (cholesterol-lowering):
    • Low intensity — fluvastatin, pravastatin, simvastatin (20–40 mg).
    • Moderate intensity — atorvastatin 10–20 mg, rosuvastatin 5–10 mg, simvastatin 40 mg.
    • High intensity — atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg.

Mechanism of Action

  1. Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase — rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis (catalyses HMG-CoA → mevalonate).
  2. Statins are structural analogues of HMG-CoA — compete for active site; ~10,000× more affinity than natural substrate.
  3. ↓ Hepatic cholesterol synthesis → hepatocytes sense low cholesterol → upregulate LDL receptor (LDLR) expression on cell surface (SREBP2 transcription factor pathway).
  4. ↑ LDLR → ↑ uptake of LDL & VLDL remnants from circulation → ↓ plasma LDL-C.
  5. ↓ Production of VLDL — reduced cholesterol for VLDL assembly.
  6. Pleiotropic effects (beyond LDL lowering):
    • ↓ Inflammation (↓ CRP; ↓ TNF-α, IL-6, MMPs).
    • ↑ Endothelial nitric oxide (NO) synthase → vasodilation.
    • ↓ Oxidative stress; ↓ oxidised LDL.
    • Plaque stabilisation — ↓ lipid content, ↓ macrophage activity, ↑ collagen.
    • ↓ Thrombosis — ↓ tissue factor, ↓ platelet aggregation.
    • Immunomodulatory — ↓ MHC-II expression.
    • ↓ Bone turnover — may reduce osteoporosis (controversial).
    • Anti-cancer (cell cycle arrest, apoptosis — investigational).

Pharmacokinetics

  • Oral; absorbed in small intestine; first-pass metabolism (liver).
  • Most are lipophilic (lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin, fluvastatin) — cross cell membranes, BBB; more muscle toxicity.
  • Pravastatin & rosuvastatin — hydrophilic; hepatic uptake transporters (OATP1B1); less muscle toxicity; less CNS effects.
  • Metabolism — simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin (CYP3A4); fluvastatin (CYP2C9); rosuvastatin, pitavastatin (minimal CYP — renal & hepatic).
  • Half-life — atorvastatin 14 h (active metabolites longer); rosuvastatin 19 h (longest); simvastatin 2–3 h; pravastatin 1.8 h; fluvastatin 1.2 h.
  • Once-daily dosing (evening preferred for short half-life — cholesterol synthesis peaks at night); atorvastatin & rosuvastatin any time.
  • Excretion — hepatic (bile, faeces); renal (pravastatin, rosuvastatin).

Lipid-Lowering Effects

Lipid Effect
LDL-C↓ 30–60% (dose-dependent; high-intensity statin lowers ≥50%)
Triglycerides↓ 10–30% (more if baseline high)
HDL-C↑ 5–10% (modest)
VLDL↓
Lp(a)No significant effect (may ↑ slightly); PCSK9 inhibitors ↓ Lp(a)

Therapeutic Uses

  1. Primary prevention — asymptomatic patients at increased CV risk; ASCVD risk ≥7.5% (ACC/AHA) or ≥10% (older); diabetes age 40–75; LDL ≥190 mg/dL.
  2. Secondary prevention — established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) — post-MI, stroke/TIA, peripheral arterial disease, revascularisation; all patients regardless of LDL.
  3. Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) — high-intensity statin started within 24 h; atorvastatin 80 mg daily; reduces recurrent events & mortality.
  4. Hypercholesterolaemia — familial (heterozygous FH); statin first-line; combination with ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor, bempedoic acid.
  5. Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia — high-dose statin + ezetimibe + PCSK9 inhibitor + lomitapide + apheresis.
  6. Stroke prevention — SPARCL trial (atorvastatin 80 mg reduced recurrent stroke in patients with prior TIA/stroke).
  7. Aortic aneurysm — may slow growth (controversial).
  8. Pre-operative statin — before major vascular surgery; reduces perioperative cardiac events.
  9. Chronic kidney disease — 4D, AURORA trials; reduced CV events in non-dialysis CKD; SHARP (simvastatin + ezetimibe) in CKD; less benefit on dialysis.
  10. Heart failure — CORONA, GISSI-HF trials; no clear benefit in established HF; statins not routinely recommended.
  11. Other emerging uses — sepsis, ARDS, cancer prevention, Alzheimer's disease, osteoporosis — investigational; routine use not recommended.

Guidelines — When to Start & Targets

Adverse Effects

  • Muscle-related (most common):
    • Myopathy — muscle pain, weakness; CK >10× ULN; risk 5–10%.
    • Myalgia — muscle pain without CK elevation; ~5–10%.
    • Myositis — muscle inflammation with CK elevation.
    • Rhabdomyolysis — severe; CK >10× ULN + myoglobinuria + AKI; rare (1/10,000); more with high doses, drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitors — macrolides, azoles, protease inhibitors, cyclosporine, gemfibrozil), hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, elderly, female, low body weight, renal/hepatic impairment, genetic (SLCO1B1 polymorphism).
    • Treatment — stop statin; hydration; monitor CK, renal function; switch to different statin or low dose; coenzyme Q10 (controversial); ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitor alternative.
  • Hepatic:
    • Transaminase elevation — 1–3%; usually transient; dose-dependent; check LFT at baseline, 3 months, then annually; stop if ALT >3× ULN.
    • Frank hepatitis — rare; usually reversible on stopping.
    • Does NOT cause liver failure (rare reports — controversial).
  • Diabetes mellitus:
    • ↑ Risk of new-onset diabetes — ~1 in 255 patients treated for 4 years; more with high-intensity statins, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome.
    • Benefit (CV risk reduction) far outweighs risk; do not stop statin.
  • Neurological:
    • Memory loss, confusion — FDA warning (controversial; evidence conflicting); reversible.
    • Peripheral neuropathy — rare; controversial.
  • GI — nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain.
  • Renal:
    • Proteinuria — rosuvastatin high dose (transient; not progressive); rarely significant.
    • Acute kidney injury — rare; from rhabdomyolysis.
  • Reproductive — contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic in animals); avoid in lactation.
  • Skin — rash, photosensitivity.
  • Haemorrhagic stroke — SPARCL trial showed small ↑ risk of haemorrhagic stroke with high-dose atorvastatin; benefit (ischaemic stroke reduction) far outweighs.
  • Other — sleep disturbance, headache, fatigue.

Drug Interactions

  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin):
    • Macrolides — erythromycin, clarithromycin (NOT azithromycin).
    • Azole antifungals — ketoconazole, itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole.
    • Protease inhibitors (HIV) — ritonavir, saquinavir.
    • Calcium channel blockers — diltiazem, verapamil (especially with simvastatin — dose limit 10–20 mg).
    • Amiodarone — simvastatin dose limit 20 mg.
    • Grapefruit juice — >1 L/day.
    • Cyclosporine — avoid with most statins; pravastatin, rosuvastatin less affected.
    • Danazol, gemfibrozil.
  • Fibrates — gemfibrozil significantly ↑ statin myopathy risk (avoid); fenofibrate safer.
  • Warfarin — ↑ INR (displacement; CYP); monitor.
  • Oral contraceptives — ↑ ethinylestradiol & norethisterone levels.
  • Digoxin — ↑ digoxin levels (atorvastatin, simvastatin — P-gp).
  • Colchicine — ↑ myopathy risk.
  • SLCO1B1 polymorphism — ↑ simvastatin myopathy risk; pharmacogenomic testing.

Monitoring

  • Lipid profile — baseline, 4–12 weeks after starting/dose change, then annually.
  • LFT — baseline, 3 months, then annually (more often if symptoms).
  • CK — baseline if risk factors; if muscle symptoms develop; not routine.
  • Renal function — baseline; if rhabdomyolysis.
  • HbA1c — monitor for new-onset diabetes (especially prediabetes).
  • Thyroid function — exclude hypothyroidism if myopathy (statin unmasking).

Combination Therapy

  • Ezetimibe — cholesterol absorption inhibitor; ↓ LDL additional 15–25%; first add-on if LDL target not met.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors — evolocumab, alirocumab (subcutaneous mAbs); ↓ LDL additional 50–60%; for FH, statin intolerance, very high-risk; FOURIER, ODYSSEY trials reduced CV events.
  • Bempedoic acid — ATP citrate lyase inhibitor; oral; ↓ LDL 15–20%; for statin intolerance.
  • Fibrates — fenofibrate (safe with statins); for hypertriglyceridaemia.

Definition

Volume of distribution (Vd) — also called apparent volume of distribution — is defined as the theoretical volume of fluid that would be required to contain the total amount of drug in the body at the same concentration as in plasma, assuming the body to be a single homogeneous compartment.

Mathematically:

Vd = (Dose administered) / (Plasma concentration at time zero, C₀)

Or after IV bolus:

Vd = Dose / C₀

For oral administration: Vd = (Dose × F) / C₀, where F = bioavailability.

Concept of Apparent Volume

  • Vd is a theoretical (apparent) volume — it does NOT correspond to any real anatomical space.
  • It is a pharmacokinetic parameter that describes how widely a drug distributes in the body relative to plasma.
  • Vd reflects the apparent space a drug "appears to occupy" based on plasma concentration.
  • If a drug remains largely in plasma (e.g., highly protein-bound, large molecule), Vd is small (close to plasma volume).
  • If a drug distributes extensively into tissues (e.g., lipid-soluble), Vd is large (may exceed total body water many-fold).

Normal Body Fluid Compartments

Compartment Volume (70 kg adult)
Plasma3 L
Blood5 L
Extracellular fluid (ECF)13–15 L
Total body water (TBW)42 L (60% body weight)

Interpretation of Vd Values

1. Low Vd (3–5 L, close to plasma volume)

  • Drug largely confined to plasma.
  • Reasons — large molecular size, high plasma protein binding, low lipid solubility, low tissue affinity.
  • Examples — heparin (large molecule), warfarin (99% albumin-bound), phenylbutazone, sulphonamides, NSAIDs, furosemide (high protein binding), monoclonal antibodies.
  • Cannot be removed by haemodialysis easily (if high protein binding).

2. Intermediate Vd (10–20 L, close to ECF)

  • Drug distributes in extracellular fluid.
  • Reasons — low lipid solubility, hydrophilic, moderate protein binding.
  • Examples — aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin — polar, hydrophilic), penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin, lithium.
  • Can be removed by haemodialysis.

3. High Vd (>40 L, may exceed body weight many-fold)

  • Drug distributes widely into tissues.
  • Reasons — high lipid solubility, low plasma protein binding, high tissue binding (especially to muscle, fat, brain).
  • Examples — digoxin (Vd ~500 L; binds to Na-K-ATPase in muscle), amiodarone (Vd ~60 L/kg; accumulates in fat), propranolol, tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), chloroquine (Vd ~100 L/kg; melanin binding), quinine, haloperidol, fluoxetine, ivermectin.
  • Vd may be hundreds of litres — this is theoretical (apparent), not real.
  • Not effectively removed by haemodialysis (drug in tissues, not plasma).

Factors Affecting Vd

  1. Lipid solubility — higher lipid solubility → higher Vd (crosses membranes, enters fat, brain).
  2. Plasma protein binding — high binding (albumin) → low Vd (drug stays in plasma); only free (unbound) drug distributes.
  3. Tissue binding — high tissue binding (muscle, fat, melanin, bone) → high Vd (digoxin, chloroquine, tetracycline in bone).
  4. Molecular size — large molecules (heparin, monoclonal antibodies) → low Vd (cannot cross capillary).
  5. Ionisation (pKa) & pH — ionised (charged) drugs do not cross lipid membranes → low Vd; trapping in compartments (pH partition — weak bases accumulate in acidic compartments like lysosomes).
  6. Permeability / blood flow — high blood flow organs (brain, heart, kidney, liver) equilibrate rapidly; low flow (fat, muscle) take longer.
  7. Disease states:
    • Heart failure — ↓ cardiac output, ↓ tissue perfusion → ↓ Vd for some drugs (lidocaine).
    • Uraemia / renal failure — ↓ protein binding (organic acids compete) → ↑ free drug → ↑ Vd for acidic drugs.
    • Cirrhosis — ↓ albumin → ↑ Vd; ascites adds volume → ↑ Vd.
    • Nephrotic syndrome — ↓ albumin → ↑ Vd.
    • Obesity — ↑ Vd for lipophilic drugs (amiodarone, diazepam, verapamil).
    • Pregnancy — ↑ plasma volume → ↑ Vd.
  8. Age:
    • Neonates — ↑ total body water, ↓ fat, immature BBB → higher Vd for water-soluble drugs.
    • Elderly — ↓ total body water, ↓ lean mass, ↑ fat → ↑ Vd for lipophilic drugs (diazepam).

Clinical Significance

  1. Loading dose calculation:
    • For drugs with high Vd or long half-life, loading dose achieves therapeutic plasma concentration rapidly.
    • Loading dose = (Vd × Target plasma concentration) / Bioavailability.
    • Example — digoxin: Vd ~7 L/kg; target 1.5 ng/mL; loading dose = 7 × 1.5 × 70 kg = 735 µg.
    • Amiodarone: loading dose 800–1600 mg/day for 1–3 weeks (large Vd).
  2. Half-life calculation:
    • t½ = (0.693 × Vd) / Clearance.
    • ↑Vd → ↑t½ (longer duration of action); e.g., amiodarone (t½ ~50 days), diazepam (t½ 30–60 h, active metabolite nordazepam ~100 h).
  3. Drug clearance:
    • Clearance = (Rate of elimination) / (Plasma concentration).
    • Vd affects drug dosing interval — high Vd → longer dosing interval.
  4. Predicting dialysability:
    • Low Vd + low protein binding + small molecule → dialysable (lithium, salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, aminoglycosides).
    • High Vd or high protein binding → not effectively dialysable (digoxin, tricyclics, phenytoin, warfarin).
  5. Predicting toxicity & overdose management:
    • High Vd drugs — large tissue stores; not removed by dialysis; may require repeated doses of antidote (e.g., digoxin — use Fab antibody).
    • Low Vd drugs — may respond to dialysis or forced diuresis.
  6. Dose adjustment in disease:
    • Volume overload (heart failure, oedema) — ↑ Vd for some drugs → may need higher dose.
    • Dehydration — ↓ Vd → higher plasma concentration → reduce dose.
  7. Drug selection in special situations:
    • CNS drugs — need to cross BBB; high lipid solubility → high Vd (diazepam, phenytoin, antidepressants).
    • Pregnancy — avoid high Vd drugs (cross placenta).

One-Compartment vs Two-Compartment Models

  • One-compartment model — drug distributes instantaneously & uniformly throughout body; plasma concentration declines monoexponentially; Vd (volume of distribution) — single value.
  • Two-compartment model — drug distributes initially into central compartment (plasma, well-perfused organs), then into peripheral compartment (fat, muscle); plasma concentration shows biexponential decline (distribution phase + elimination phase).
  • Vc (central compartment volume) — initial volume; Vd(ss) (steady-state Vd); Vd(extrapolated) / Vd(β) — calculated by extrapolating elimination phase to time zero; Vd(ss) preferred.

Clinical Pearl

Vd is a theoretical (apparent) volume — not a real anatomical space. Drugs with low Vd (3–5 L) are confined to plasma — large molecules (heparin), highly protein-bound (warfarin, NSAIDs); drugs with intermediate Vd (10–20 L) distribute in ECF — aminoglycosides, penicillins, lithium; drugs with high Vd (>40 L, may exceed body weight) distribute widely in tissues — digoxin (Vd 500 L), amiodarone (Vd 60 L/kg), tricyclic antidepressants, chloroquine. Vd affects: loading dose calculation (high Vd needs high loading dose), half-life (t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Clearance), dialysability (low Vd + low protein binding = dialysable), and toxicity management. Always check Vd before recommending haemodialysis in overdose — digoxin (Vd 500 L, 25% protein-bound) is NOT removed by dialysis; use Fab antibody. Lithium (Vd ~0.6 L/kg, no protein binding) IS removed by dialysis. Disease states alter Vd — heart failure ↓ Vd (reduced perfusion); uraemia ↑ Vd (↓ protein binding of acidic drugs); cirrhosis ↑ Vd (↓ albumin, ascites); obesity ↑ Vd for lipophilic drugs (amiodarone, diazepam). Always adjust dose in disease — dehydrated patients may need lower dose (↓ Vd → ↑ plasma concentration); overloaded patients may need higher dose (↑ Vd).

  • Identify & treat precipitant — hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoxia, sepsis, CNS infection, trauma, drug withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines), drug toxicity (TCAs, theophylline), eclampsia, tumour, stroke.
  • Send blood for — CBG, glucose, electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, Mg), LFT, RFT, ABG, toxicology, AED levels (if on treatment), cultures if infection suspected.
  • EEG monitoring — if seizures persist despite treatment; for non-convulsive status.

  • Immunotherapy — IV methylprednisolone, IVIG, plasmapheresis (if autoimmune — anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1, anti-GABA-A encephalitis).

  • Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) — case reports; for refractory.

  • Transplant patients — levetiracetam (no interactions); avoid valproate, phenytoin (interactions with immunosuppressants).

  • Neurological — hippocampal sclerosis; cognitive impairment; recurrent seizures; permanent neurological deficit.
  • Respiratory — aspiration pneumonia, ARDS, respiratory failure.
  • Cardiovascular — arrhythmias, hypertension/hypotension, cardiac arrest.
  • Metabolic — acidosis, hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis (CK), AKI.
  • Hyperthermia.
  • Thromboembolism (DVT prophylaxis).
  • Pressure sores, infections (line, urinary, respiratory).
  • Mortality 10–30%; worse with longer duration, elderly, comorbidities.

Status epilepticus is a medical emergency — every minute of ongoing seizure increases neuronal damage. Algorithm: Stabilise ABC + glucose/thiamine → IV lorazepam 4 mg (or IM midazolam 10 mg if no IV) at 5 min → IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg OR fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg OR valproate 40 mg/kg at 10–30 min → if refractory, intubate + continuous midazolam/propofol/pentobarbital infusion to burst suppression on EEG at 30–60 min. Continuous EEG monitoring essential in refractory & super-refractory — goal is burst suppression for 24–48 h before tapering anaesthesia. Magnesium sulphate is drug of choice for eclampsia — not benzodiazepine; also reduces BP. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) for isoniazid overdose — 1 g per gram INH; also rare pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy in neonates. India — SE common; non-compliance with AED is leading cause; access to ICU & EEG limited; levetiracetam increasingly preferred (no interactions, no hepatic metabolism); valproate widely used (cheap, broad-spectrum) but avoid in pregnancy.

Introduction

β1-selective (cardioselective) blockers — atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, esmolol — preferentially block β1-adrenergic receptors in the heart over β2 receptors in the lungs, blood vessels, & metabolism. They are preferred over non-selective β-blockers (propranolol) in hypertension with comorbid conditions where β2 blockade is harmful (asthma, COPD, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease).

Mechanism of β1 Selectivity

  1. β1 receptors — located primarily in heart (SA node, AV node, atria, ventricles), juxtaglomerular cells of kidney (renin release).
  2. β2 receptors — located in bronchi (bronchodilation), skeletal muscle blood vessels (vasodilation), liver (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis), pancreas (insulin release), uterus (relaxation), mast cells (stabilisation).
  3. Cardioselective β-blockers have higher affinity for β1 than β2 (ratio 10–50:1) — at low doses, predominantly β1 blockade; at high doses, selectivity lost (some β2 blockade).
  4. Selectivity is dose-dependent — lost at high doses; even atenolol/metoprolol can cause bronchospasm in high doses in asthmatics.

Pharmacological Rationale for β1-Selective Blockers in Hypertension

1. Effective BP Reduction

  • ↓ Cardiac output — β1 blockade on SA node & AV node → ↓ heart rate (negative chronotropy), ↓ contractility (negative inotropy), ↓ conduction (negative dromotropy) → ↓ cardiac output (15–20%) → ↓ BP.
  • ↓ Renin release — β1 blockade on juxtaglomerular cells → ↓ renin → ↓ angiotensin II → ↓ aldosterone → ↓ Na & water retention → ↓ blood volume → ↓ BP.
  • ↓ Central sympathetic outflow (especially lipophilic — metoprolol, propranolol) — crosses BBB → ↓ sympathetic tone from vasomotor centre.
  • ↓ Norepinephrine release — presynaptic β2 blockade (less than non-selective) reduces facilitation of norepinephrine release.
  • Onset of BP effect — hours; full effect in 1–2 weeks; suitable for chronic hypertension.

2. Cardioprotective Effects

  • ↓ Myocardial oxygen demand — ↓ HR & contractility → ↓ oxygen consumption; useful in coexisting angina.
  • Antiarrhythmic — class II antiarrhythmic; ↓ AV nodal conduction; useful for AF rate control, SVT, ventricular ectopics; ↓ post-MI arrhythmias.
  • ↓ Mortality post-MI — reduces reinfarction, sudden cardiac death; metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol proven.
  • Improve survival in heart failure — bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (HFrEF); start low, go slow, aim high.
  • Reverse cardiac remodelling — ↓ LVH in chronic hypertension.

3. Advantages of β1 Selectivity Over Non-Selective β-Blockers

a. Respiratory — Bronchospasm
  • Non-selective β-blockers (propranolol) block β2-mediated bronchodilation → bronchospasm in asthma/COPD; potentially fatal.
  • Cardioselective β-blockers spare β2 → less bronchoconstriction; safer in mild-moderate asthma & COPD; but still caution — selectivity lost at high doses.
  • Trials (MERIT-HF, COPD subgroup) — metoprolol & bisoprolol safe in COPD with cardiac indication.
  • Nebivolol — most β1-selective; additional NO-mediated vasodilation.
b. Metabolic — Glucose Homeostasis
  • Non-selective β-blockers block β2-mediated glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, glucagon release → ↓ recovery from hypoglycaemia; mask hypoglycaemia symptoms (tremor, palpitations) except sweating; dangerous in diabetics on insulin/sulfonylureas.
  • Cardioselective β-blockers have less effect on glucose recovery & symptom masking; safer in diabetics; also less effect on lipid profile (less ↑ triglycerides, less ↓ HDL).
  • Carvedilol (α1 + β) — best metabolic profile; improves insulin sensitivity; preferred in diabetics with hypertension or HF.
c. Peripheral Vascular
  • Non-selective β-blockers block β2-mediated vasodilation in skeletal muscle → unopposed α-mediated vasoconstriction → cold extremities, Raynaud's worsening, claudication in PAD.
  • Cardioselective β-blockers spare β2 → less peripheral vasoconstriction; safer in mild PAD, Raynaud's.
  • Carvedilol & labetalol (α1 + β) — vasodilation from α1 blockade; preferred in PAD, diabetes.
  • Nebivolol — NO-mediated vasodilation; preferred in elderly, metabolic syndrome, peripheral vascular disease.
d. Lipid Profile
  • Non-selective β-blockers — ↑ triglycerides, ↓ HDL; worsen metabolic profile.
  • Cardioselective β-blockers — less effect; carvedilol, nebivolol — neutral or improve.
e. Exercise Tolerance
  • Non-selective β-blockers ↓ exercise capacity more (β2 blockade in muscle blood flow & glycogenolysis).
  • Cardioselective β-blockers less effect; preferred in athletes.

4. Special Indications for β1-Selective Blockers in Hypertension

Limitations of β1-Selective Blockers in Hypertension

  • Less effective than ACEI/ARB, CCB, thiazide for stroke prevention (LIFE, ASCOT trials — losartan & amlodipine superior to atenolol); not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
  • Less effective in elderly & Black patients (low renin state).
  • Selectivity lost at high doses — even atenolol/metoprolol can cause bronchospasm in severe asthma.
  • Side effects — fatigue, dizziness, sexual dysfunction, sleep disturbance, depression (especially lipophilic — metoprolol, propranolol).
  • Metabolic effects — ↑ triglycerides, ↓ HDL (less than non-selective but still present); ↑ risk of new-onset diabetes (especially with thiazide combination).
  • Rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal — taper gradually.

Guidelines — When β1-Selective Blockers Are Preferred

  • NICE, ESC, ACC/AHA — β-blockers NOT first-line for uncomplicated hypertension; reserved for compelling cardiac indications.
  • Compelling indications:
    • Post-MI.
    • Heart failure (HFrEF).
    • Angina.
    • Atrial fibrillation.
    • Aortic aneurysm/dissection.
    • HOCM.
    • Long QT syndrome.
  • Preferred in hypertension with:
    • Coexisting cardiac disease (post-MI, HF, angina, AF).
    • Hyperthyroidism (propranolol preferred).
    • Migraine.
    • Essential tremor.
    • Pregnancy (labetalol).
    • Perioperative.

Clinical Pearl

β1-selective (cardioselective) blockers are preferred over non-selective β-blockers when β2 blockade is undesirable — asthma/COPD (avoid bronchospasm), diabetes (avoid masking hypoglycaemia & impaired recovery), peripheral vascular disease/Raynaud's (avoid vasoconstriction), elderly (less CNS & metabolic effects). Selectivity is dose-dependent — lost at high doses; even atenolol/metoprolol can cause bronchospasm in severe asthma; use lowest effective dose; consider alternative if asthma severe. β-blockers are NOT first-line for uncomplicated hypertension — ACEI/ARB, CCB, thiazide preferred; β-blockers reserved for compelling cardiac indications (post-MI, HF, angina, AF) or specific situations (hyperthyroidism, migraine, pregnancy, perioperative). Only bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol have proven mortality benefit in heart failure — start low, go slow, aim high (target dose). Carvedilol (α1 + β) is preferred in diabetes — improves insulin sensitivity, neutral metabolic, vasodilation. Nebivolol is preferred in elderly — NO-mediated vasodilation, most β1-selective, less fatigue, less sexual dysfunction. Labetalol is preferred in pregnancy — α1 + β; safe, effective, first-line. Avoid abrupt cessation — rebound hypertension, tachycardia, MI; taper over 1–2 weeks. Always check for contraindications — severe asthma, 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sinus bradycardia, decompensated HF, severe PAD, hypotension, phaeochromocytoma (without α-blockade). India — atenolol widely used & cheap (though less evidence than newer); metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol available; nebivolol more expensive; underutilised in HF despite proven benefit; physician education about "start low, go slow, aim high" in HF.
