Definition

Anticoagulants are drugs that prevent or reduce the coagulation (clotting) of blood — used in prevention & treatment of thromboembolic disorders (DVT, PE, atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves, ACS).

Classification of Anticoagulants (3 marks)

A. Parenteral Anticoagulants

  1. Indirect thrombin inhibitors (acting via antithrombin):
    • Heparin (Unfractionated Heparin, UFH) — IV/SC; inhibits thrombin (IIa) & factor Xa via antithrombin (AT).
    • Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) — enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin; SC; preferentially inhibit factor Xa > thrombin.
    • Fondaparinux — synthetic pentasaccharide; selective factor Xa inhibitor via antithrombin; SC.
    • Idraparinux, idrabiotaparinux — long-acting pentasaccharides (investigational).
  2. Direct thrombin inhibitors (do not require antithrombin):
    • Lepirudin, desirudin — recombinant hirudin (from leech); IV/SC; for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
    • Bivalirudin — hirudin analogue; IV; PCI, HIT.
    • Argatroban — small molecule; IV; HIT.

B. Oral Anticoagulants

  1. Vitamin K Antagonists (Coumarins):
    • Warfarin — most common; racemic mixture.
    • A cenocoumarol — shorter half-life; used in Europe, India.
    • Phenprocoumon — longer half-life; Europe.
    • Dicoumarol, ethyl biscoumacetate — historical.
  2. Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs / NOACs / Target-Specific Oral Anticoagulants):
    • Direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor — Dabigatran (Pradaxa).
    • Direct factor Xa inhibitors:
      • Rivaroxaban (Xarelto).
      • Apixaban (Eliquis).
      • Edoxaban (Lixiana, Savaysa).
      • Betrixaban (Bevyxxa) — withdrawn.

C. Other Anticoagulants

  • Defibrotide — purified polydeoxyribonucleotide; modulates endothelial function; hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD) post-HSCT.
  • Antithrombin concentrate — for AT deficiency; heparin resistance.
  • Protein C concentrate — purpura fulminans (homozygous protein C deficiency).
  • Thrombomodulin (recombinant soluble) — sepsis-associated DIC (historical).
  • Sulodexide — glycosaminoglycan; diabetic nephropathy (investigational).

Heparin (5 marks)

Source & Chemistry

  • Naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan (mucopolysaccharide); extracted from porcine intestinal mucosa or bovine lung.
  • Mixture of sulphated polysaccharides; MW 3,000–30,000 Da (average 15,000).
  • Strongly negatively charged (sulphate groups) — basis for neutralisation by protamine sulphate (positively charged).

Mechanism of Action

  1. Heparin binds to antithrombin III (AT) (endogenous serine protease inhibitor) via a specific pentasaccharide sequence.
  2. Binding induces conformational change in AT → exposes active site → accelerates AT-mediated inhibition of clotting factors (1000-fold).
  3. Inactivates thrombin (IIa), factor Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa, kallikrein.
  4. Unfractionated heparin inhibits both thrombin & factor Xa equally (1:1 ratio).
  5. LMWH (<6500 Da) — preferentially inhibits factor Xa (ratio ~3–4:1) — cannot simultaneously bind thrombin & AT (short chain).
  6. Fondaparinux — pure pentasaccharide; exclusively inhibits factor Xa.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Not absorbed orally (large, charged molecule); given IV or SC.
  • Onset — IV immediate; SC 1–2 h.
  • Half-life — 1–2 h (dose-dependent; longer at high doses); 60–90 min after IV bolus.
  • Metabolism — hepatic (heparinase) & reticuloendothelial; partial renal excretion.
  • Does not cross placenta (large molecule) — safe in pregnancy.
  • Monitoring — aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time); target 1.5–2.5× control. LMWH does not require routine monitoring (predictable pharmacokinetics); monitor anti-Xa level in pregnancy, renal impairment, obesity, children.
  • Antidote — protamine sulphate 1 mg neutralises 100 U heparin (given IV slowly; risk of hypotension, anaphylaxis).

Therapeutic Uses

  • Venous thromboembolism (VTE) — DVT & PE — acute & long-term.
  • Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) — unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI (with antiplatelets).
  • PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention) — UFH or bivalirudin.
  • Atrial fibrillation — cardioversion (if not on warfarin/DOAC); bridging therapy.
  • Mechanical heart valves — perioperative bridging.
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass, haemodialysis, extracorporeal circuits — anticoagulation.
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — selected cases (with bleeding).
  • Pregnancy — LMWH for VTE prophylaxis/treatment, mechanical heart valves, antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).
  • Heparin flushes — IV catheter patency.

Adverse Effects

  • Bleeding — most common; dose-dependent; monitor aPTT; reverse with protamine.
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT):
    • Immune-mediated (IgG antibody against heparin-platelet factor 4 [PF4] complex).
    • Type I — mild, non-immune, early (days 1–4), platelet count >100,000; not clinically significant.
    • Type II — severe, immune-mediated, 5–14 days after exposure (or sooner if previous exposure); platelet count <100,000 (or 50% drop); paradoxical thrombosis (arterial & venous) — limb gangrene, stroke, PE; STOP heparin immediately; switch to direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin) or fondaparinux; never re-expose to heparin.
    • Diagnosis — clinical (4T score) + laboratory (PF4 ELISA, serotonin release assay [SRA]).
    • LMWH has lower risk than UFH but still contraindicated once HIT develops.
  • Osteoporosis — long-term use (>1 month); ↓ bone formation, ↑ bone resorption; vertebral fractures; mechanism — osteoclast activation, ↓ osteocalcin.
  • Hypoaldosteronism & hyperkalaemia — heparin inhibits aldosterone synthesis; rare but significant in renal impairment, diabetes.
  • Hypersensitivity reactions — urticaria, anaphylaxis, bronchospasm (bovine source higher risk).
  • Skin necrosis — rare; at injection sites; may precede HIT.
  • Withdrawal rebound — possible thrombosis after abrupt cessation; taper.
  • Elevated liver transaminases — common, benign.
  • Priapism — rare.

Contraindications

  • Active bleeding (GI, intracranial, etc.).
  • Severe bleeding diathesis (haemophilia, thrombocytopenia <50,000).
  • Recent neurosurgery, ophthalmic surgery, intracranial haemorrhage.
  • Severe uncontrolled hypertension.
  • Bacterial endocarditis (risk of mycotic aneurysm rupture).
  • HIT (current or past).
  • Known hypersensitivity (porcine or bovine).

Warfarin (5 marks)

Source & Chemistry

  • 4-Hydroxycoumarin derivative; synthetic; racemic mixture of R- & S-enantiomers (S more potent).
  • Discovered as cause of haemorrhagic disease in cattle (sweet clover disease — dicoumarol from spoiled sweet clover; Link, 1940s); warfarin developed as rat poison (1948); first used clinically in 1954.
  • Oral; highly protein-bound (99%); small volume of distribution.

Mechanism of Action

  1. Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) — enzyme that recycles oxidised vitamin K (vitamin K 2,3-epoxide) back to active reduced form (hydroquinone, KH2).
  2. ↓ Active vitamin K → ↓ γ-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
  3. Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors — II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X; also protein C & protein S (endogenous anticoagulants).
  4. γ-carboxylation (by γ-glutamyl carboxylase) adds carboxyl groups to glutamic acid residues → γ-carboxyglutamic acid (GLA) → enables calcium binding → anchors factors to phospholipid surfaces → active clotting.
  5. Without γ-carboxylation, factors are dysfunctional (PIVKA — Proteins Induced by Vitamin K Antagonism).
  6. Onset of action — slow (8–12 h for factor VII; 2–7 days for full anticoagulation) — due to long half-life of existing carboxylated factors (II: 60 h, X: 24–48 h, VII: 6 h, IX: 24 h).
  7. Protein C has shortest half-life (8 h) — its levels fall first → transient procoagulant state → skin necrosis in deficient patients.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Rapid & complete oral absorption; bioavailability ~100%.
  • 99% bound to plasma albumin; small Vd (~0.14 L/kg).
  • Hepatic metabolism — CYP2C9 (S-warfarin, more potent); CYP1A2, CYP3A4 (R-warfarin).
  • Half-life — 36–42 h; long duration of action.
  • Crosses placenta — teratogenic (contraindicated in pregnancy).
  • Monitoring — PT (Prothrombin Time) / INR (International Normalised Ratio).
    • Target INR — 2.0–3.0 for most indications (DVT, PE, AF, mechanical bioprosthetic valve); 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valve, recurrent VTE on warfarin, antiphospholipid syndrome.
    • Initial dose — 5 mg/day (2.5 mg if elderly, liver disease, malnourished); adjust based on INR at 3, 7, 14 days, then monthly.
  • Antidote — vitamin K1 (phytonadione) (oral, SC, IV — slow); FFP (fresh frozen plasma); PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate — four-factor preferred); recombinant factor VIIa (refractory).

Therapeutic Uses

  • VTE (DVT & PE) — treatment & secondary prevention — 3–6 months (provoked) or lifelong (unprovoked, recurrent, cancer, thrombophilia).
  • Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women).
  • Mechanical heart valves — lifelong; mitral valve target INR 3.0 (range 2.5–3.5); aortic valve 2.5 (range 2.0–3.0).
  • Bioprosthetic valves — 3–6 months after implantation (then aspirin).
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome — lifelong; INR 2.5–3.5.
  • LV thrombus, mural thrombus post-MI — 3–6 months.
  • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — 3–12 months.
  • Peripheral arterial disease — selected cases (with antiplatelet).

Adverse Effects

  • Bleeding — most common; dose-dependent; risk increases with INR >4, age, concomitant antiplatelet/NSAID, comorbidities; reverse with vitamin K, FFP, PCC based on severity & INR.
  • Skin necrosis:
    • Rare (~0.01–0.1%); occurs 3–10 days after starting warfarin.
    • Due to depletion of protein C (shortest half-life — 8 h) before procoagulant factors (II, X) fall → transient procoagulant state → microvascular thrombosis in skin (breasts, buttocks, thighs, penis).
    • Higher risk in protein C deficiency (congenital or acquired).
    • Prevention — "bridge" with heparin (UFH/LMWH) until INR therapeutic for 2 days; start warfarin at low dose (2.5–5 mg); check protein C level if family history.
    • Treatment — stop warfarin; give vitamin K; heparin; FFP/PCC; protein C concentrate if deficient.
  • Teratogenicity:
    • Contraindicated in pregnancy (crosses placenta).
    • 1st trimester — embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia, ocular abnormalities); "warfarin embryopathy" — risk 5–10% if exposed weeks 6–12.
    • 2nd & 3rd trimester — foetal bleeding, CNS abnormalities (Dandy-Walker malformation, optic atrophy), miscarriage, stillbirth.
    • Use LMWH in pregnancy; switch back to warfarin postpartum (safe in breastfeeding).
  • Purple toe syndrome — rare; cholesterol microembolisation; painful purple toes; stop warfarin.
  • Hair loss, rash, fever, GI upset — uncommon.
  • Hepatotoxicity — rare; cholestatic.
  • Tracheal calcification, osteoporosis — long-term; rare.

Warfarin has the most drug interactions of any medication — due to high protein binding, narrow therapeutic index, hepatic metabolism, gut flora effects.

  • Enhanced anticoagulation (↑ INR, bleeding risk):
    • CYP2C9 inhibitors — amiodarone, fluconazole, metronidazole, miconazole, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, fluvoxamine, phenytoin (variable).
    • CYP3A4 inhibitors — macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), azole antifungals, protease inhibitors, grapefruit juice.

    • Additive bleeding risk — antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel), NSAIDs, SSRIs.
    • Alcohol — acutely inhibits metabolism (↑ INR); chronically induces enzymes (↓ INR).
  • Reduced anticoagulation (↓ INR, thrombosis risk):
    • CYP inducers — rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, griseofulvin, St John's wort, nevirapine.
    • ↑ Vitamin K intake — green leafy vegetables, supplements, enteral feeds.
    • Reduced absorption — cholestyramine, sucralfate, antacids.
    • Genetic — VKORC1 polymorphisms (require lower dose); CYP2C9 polymorphisms (slow metabolism, lower dose).

  • Predictable pharmacokinetics — no routine monitoring (no INR).
  • Rapid onset (2–4 h) — no heparin bridging.
  • Short half-life — quick offset.
  • Few drug interactions (CYP3A4/P-gp).
  • No dietary vitamin K restriction.
  • Lower intracranial haemorrhage risk than warfarin (in AF trials).

Disadvantages

  • Renal excretion — dose adjustment in CKD; avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 for dabigatran, <15 for rivaroxaban/apixaban).
  • Cost — expensive vs warfarin.
  • No routine monitoring — compliance concern.
  • Antidotes expensive & not always available.
  • Higher GI bleeding risk than warfarin (especially dabigatran, rivaroxaban).
  • Not recommended in pregnancy, mechanical heart valves (RE-ALIGN trial — dabigatran worse than warfarin).
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome with triple positivity — warfarin preferred.

Clinical Pearl

Heparin & warfarin have different mechanisms — heparin potentiates antithrombin (immediate); warfarin inhibits vitamin K recycling (slow onset, days). Always bridge with heparin when starting warfarin — 5–7 days overlap until INR therapeutic for 2 consecutive days, then stop heparin. Warfarin skin necrosis — occurs in first week; due to protein C depletion (shortest half-life) before procoagulant factors fall → transient procoagulant state; higher risk in protein C deficiency; prevent with heparin bridging & low starting dose. HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) type II — paradoxical thrombosis 5–14 days after heparin; platelet count drops >50%; STOP all heparin immediately; switch to argatroban or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitors); never re-expose to heparin/LMWH. Warfarin is teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy; use LMWH (does not cross placenta). Always check INR before surgery/procedure — stop warfarin 5 days before; bridge with LMWH if high thrombotic risk (mechanical valve, recent VTE, AF with high CHA2DS2-VASc). DOACs are replacing warfarin for most indications (AF, VTE) — no monitoring, no dietary restriction, fewer interactions, lower intracranial bleed. However, warfarin remains preferred for — mechanical heart valves, severe renal impairment, antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive), pregnancy (LMWH preferred actually), patients with poor adherence (warfarin's long half-life is forgiving). Reversal — warfarin: vitamin K + FFP or PCC (4-factor preferred); heparin: protamine; dabigatran: idarucizumab; rivaroxaban/apixaban: andexanet alfa; all: supportive care, activated charcoal if recent ingestion. India — warfarin widely used (low cost); DOACs increasingly available but expensive; generic apixaban launched 2023 — improving affordability.

Definition

Status asthmaticus (acute severe asthma) is a life-threatening exacerbation of asthma that is unresponsive to standard initial treatment (inhaled β2-agonist + ipratropium + systemic corticosteroid). It can progress to respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, and death. Severe acute asthma without response to initial therapy is also called "acute severe asthma" or "refractory asthma".

Assessment — Severity

SpO₂≥92%<92%<92% + ↓ conscious level
SpeechNormalSentencesWords / unable
RR↑≥25/minBradypnoea / exhaustion

PaO₂ (kPa)Normal<8<8
PaCO₂ (kPa)<4.6<6≥6 (rising)

Signs of Imminent Respiratory Arrest

  • Silent chest (no breath sounds despite effort).
  • Cyanosis, SpO₂ <92% despite O₂.
  • Bradycardia, hypotension.
  • Exhaustion, altered consciousness, confusion, coma.
  • Paradoxical breathing, abdominal breathing.
  • Arrhythmia.

Pharmacotherapy

1. Oxygen

  • 100% oxygen via face mask (or nasal cannula at high flow) to maintain SpO₂ >94% (or 91–95% in COPD overlap).
  • Target PaO₂ >60 mmHg (8 kPa).
  • Monitor — pulse oximetry, ABG.

2. Short-Acting β2-Agonists (SABA) — First-Line

  • Salbutamol (albuterol):
    • Nebulised — 2.5–5 mg (5 mg in severe) every 20 min × 3 doses in first hour; then 5–10 mg every hour or continuous nebulisation (10–15 mg/h).
    • MDI with spacer — 4–8 puffs (100 µg each) every 20 min × 3 doses; suitable for less severe.
    • IV (rarely needed) — 5 µg/kg loading over 10 min, then 0.1–0.2 µg/kg/min infusion; titrate to effect; risk of tachycardia, hypokalaemia, lactic acidosis.
    • Mechanism — β2 agonist → ↑ cAMP → bronchodilation; relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, inhibits mast cell mediator release, ↑ mucociliary clearance.
  • Levosalbutamol (R-salbutamol) — active enantiomer; 1.25–2.5 mg nebulised; may have fewer side effects.
  • Terbutaline — alternative; 5–10 mg nebulised; SC 0.25 mg.

3. Anticholinergics — Added to SABA

  • Ipratropium bromide:
    • Nebulised — 0.5 mg every 20 min × 3 doses in first hour; then 0.5 mg every 4–6 h.
    • MDI with spacer — 4–8 puffs every 20 min × 3 doses.
    • Mechanism — muscarinic (M3) antagonist → ↓ cGMP → bronchodilation; reduces mucus secretion; additive to SABA.
  • Combination — salbutamol 2.5 mg + ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised every 20 min × 3 (Combivent); preferred in severe.

4. Systemic Corticosteroids — Essential for All Severe Exacerbations

  • Reduce inflammation, oedema, mucus; prevent relapse; onset 4–6 h.
  • Hydrocortisone — 100–200 mg IV every 6 h (loading 4 mg/kg); preferred for severe / unable to take oral.
  • Methylprednisolone — 40–60 mg IV every 6 h (or 1–2 mg/kg/day); alternative.
  • Prednisolone — 40–60 mg PO daily (if tolerating oral); equivalent efficacy to IV.
  • Duration — 5–10 days; taper not necessary for short course.
  • Early administration (within 1 h) reduces hospitalisation & mortality.

5. Magnesium Sulphate — Adjunct for Severe

  • IV Magnesium sulphate — 2 g (1–2 g) IV over 20 min (in adults; 25–50 mg/kg in children max 2 g); bronchodilator (inhibits Ca²⁺ influx, stabilises mast cells).
  • Indications — severe exacerbation not responding to SABA + ipratropium + steroid; PEF <50% predicted; life-threatening features.
  • Adverse effects — flushing, hypotension, weakness; monitor BP, reflexes; avoid in renal failure (or reduce dose).
  • Nebulised magnesium (isotonic) — 3 × 500 mg doses in first hour; less effective than IV but no systemic effects.

6. Methylxanthines — Second-Line (Historical)

  • IV Aminophylline:
    • 5 mg/kg loading over 20 min (if not on theophylline); then 0.5–0.7 mg/kg/h infusion.
    • Monitor serum theophylline (target 10–15 µg/mL); narrow therapeutic window.
    • Less effective than SABA; more adverse effects (arrhythmia, seizures, GI); rarely used now; reserved for refractory.
  • Theophylline (oral) — for chronic; not for acute severe.

7. Ketamine — Adjunct / Anaesthetic

  • Dissociative anaesthetic with bronchodilator properties.
  • IV 0.5–1 mg/kg loading then 0.5–2 mg/kg/h infusion.
  • Useful for — severe bronchospasm requiring intubation; facilitates intubation without compromising bronchodilation.
  • Adverse — hypertension, tachycardia, emergence reactions, increased secretions (combine with antisialogogue).

8. Heliox — Adjunct

  • Helium-oxygen mixture (80:20 or 70:30) — lower density than air → reduces work of breathing; improves airflow in narrowed airways (laminar flow).
  • Useful for — severe airflow obstruction not responding to standard therapy; bridge to mechanical ventilation.
  • Limited by — need for >30% oxygen (heliox requires >20% oxygen minimum).

9. Inhalational Anaesthetics — Last Resort

  • Isoflurane, sevoflurane, halothane, enflurane — bronchodilator; useful in refractory status asthmaticus on mechanical ventilation.
  • Administered via anaesthesia machine; intensive monitoring; ICU.
  • Adverse — hypotension, arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia (halothane).

10. Other Adjuncts

  • Antibiotics — only if bacterial infection suspected (fever, purulent sputum, infiltrate on X-ray); not routine.
  • Sedation — for intubated patients; propofol, midazolam, fentanyl (avoid histamine-releasing — morphine, meperidine).
  • Neuromuscular blockade — vecuronium, rocuronium; for ventilator dyssynchrony.
  • Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) — for refractory hypercapnia/hypoxaemia; last resort.
  • Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) — IV preparation (in trials); role unclear.
  • Anti-IgE (omalizumab), anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab, benralizumab), anti-IL-4Rα (dupilumab) — for chronic severe eosinophilic asthma; not for acute.

Non-Pharmacological Management

  • Mechanical ventilation — for respiratory failure, exhaustion, altered consciousness; permissive hypercapnia (low tidal volume 4–8 mL/kg, slow rate 10–14/min, short inspiratory time, long expiratory time to avoid air-trapping); deep sedation ± paralysis.
  • Non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) — controversial; may benefit carefully selected patients with hypercapnia but risk of deterioration.
  • Fluids — IV fluids to maintain hydration (may be needed due to poor intake, tachypnoea); avoid overload (pulmonary oedema).
  • Electrolytes — correct hypokalaemia (β2-agonist effect), hypomagnesaemia.
  • Monitoring — continuous SpO₂, ECG, BP, PEF (if cooperative), ABG; watch for fatigue, silent chest, hypercapnia.

Triggers to Identify & Treat

  • Respiratory infection (viral URI — rhinovirus, RSV, influenza; bacterial).
  • Allergen exposure — dust mites, pollen, animal dander, mould.
  • Non-compliance with controller medication (ICS).
  • NSAIDs, β-blockers, aspirin (in susceptible patients).
  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
  • Exercise, cold air, emotional stress.
  • Smoking (active or passive).
  • Occupational exposure.
  • Food additives — sulfites.

Discharge & Follow-Up

  • Continue prednisolone 40–60 mg/day for 5–10 days.
  • Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) — long-acting; beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone, ciclesonide; the cornerstone of chronic therapy.
  • ICS + LABA (long-acting β2-agonist) — combination inhaler (fluticasone + salmeterol; budesonide + formoterol); for moderate-severe persistent asthma.
  • SABA — reliever; salbutamol MDI for symptom relief.
  • Asthma action plan — written; peak flow monitoring; recognise & respond to exacerbations.
  • Follow-up — within 1–4 weeks; assess control; adjust stepwise.
  • Education — inhaler technique; trigger avoidance; smoking cessation; vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal).

Clinical Pearl

Status asthmaticus is a medical emergency — recognise severity early (PEF, SpO₂, speech, RR, HR, ABG); silent chest & rising PaCO₂ are signs of impending arrest. First-line therapy: 100% oxygen + nebulised salbutamol (5 mg) + ipratropium (0.5 mg) every 20 min × 3 doses + systemic corticosteroid (hydrocortisone 100–200 mg IV or prednisolone 40–60 mg PO). IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 20 min for severe unresponsive cases — bronchodilator; well-tolerated. Avoid IV aminophylline if possible — narrow therapeutic index, seizures, arrhythmia; less effective than SABA. Indications for intubation — altered consciousness, exhaustion, silent chest, PaCO₂ rising (>45 mmHg), severe hypoxaemia despite maximal therapy. Mechanical ventilation strategy — permissive hypercapnia (low tidal volume 6 mL/kg, slow rate 10/min, long expiratory time); avoid air-trapping (auto-PEEP); deep sedation ± paralysis. Nebulised salbutamol continues during mechanical ventilation — inline nebuliser in circuit. Inhalational anaesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane) — refractory cases; bronchodilator; ICU with anaesthesia machine. ECMO — last resort; refractory hypercapnia/hypoxaemia. Always identify & treat trigger — infection (antibiotics only if bacterial), allergen, NSAID, non-compliance. Discharge on ICS (or ICS + LABA) + SABA reliever + 5-day prednisolone + asthma action plan + follow-up. India — asthma mortality high; access to ICS limited; overuse of SABA & underuse of ICS; affordability & education critical. Asthma deaths are largely preventable with proper chronic controller therapy (ICS) & early aggressive treatment of exacerbations.

Introduction

Diuretics increase urine output by inhibiting sodium reabsorption at different segments of the nephron. Classified by site of action & mechanism.

Classification by Site of Action

1. Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)

  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors — Acetazolamide; inhibit CA → ↓ H⁺ secretion → ↓ NaHCO₃ reabsorption → mild diuresis; metabolic acidosis. Used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, metabolic alkalosis, epilepsy.
  • Adenosine A1 receptor antagonists — (investigational — rolofylline, failed trials); aquaretics.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors — Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin; inhibit Na-glucose cotransporter in PCT → glucosuria, natriuresis; primarily for diabetes, heart failure.

2. Thick Ascending Limb of Loop of Henle (TAL)

  • Loop diuretics (high-ceiling) — Furosemide, Bumetanide, Torsemide, Ethacrynic acid, Piretanide; inhibit Na-K-2Cl (NKCC2) cotransporter → ↑ Na, K, Cl, Ca, Mg excretion; potent diuresis (20–25% filtered Na); used for oedema, HF, AKI, hypercalcaemia.

3. Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)

  • Thiazides & thiazide-like — Hydrochlorothiazide, Chlorthalidone, Indapamide, Metolazone, Chlorothiazide, Bendroflumethiazide; inhibit Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC); moderate diuresis (5–10% filtered Na); used for hypertension, oedema, osteoporosis, diabetes insipidus.

4. Cortical Collecting Duct (CCD)

  • Potassium-sparing diuretics:
    • Aldosterone antagonists (competitive) — Spironolactone, Eplerenone, Canrenone; block mineralocorticoid receptor → ↓ Na reabsorption, ↓ K & H excretion; used for HF, resistant HTN, primary aldosteronism, ascites.
    • ENaC blockers (non-competitive) — Amiloride, Triamterene; block epithelial Na channel (ENaC); used with thiazide to prevent hypokalaemia; lithium-induced nephrogenic DI (amiloride).

5. Other

  • Osmotic diuretics — Mannitol, Urea; filtered but not reabsorbed → osmotic retention of water in tubule; used for raised ICP, raised IOP, AKI prevention.
  • Vasopressin antagonists (aquaretics) — Tolvaptan, Conivaptan, Lixivaptan; block V2 receptor → free water excretion; for SIADH, hyponatraemia, ADPKD (tolvaptan).
  • Adenosine receptor antagonists — Theophylline (mild); caffeine.

Mechanism of Thiazide Diuretics

  1. Inhibit Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) — apical membrane; site of 5–10% of filtered Na reabsorption.
  2. Thiazides compete with Cl⁻ binding site; inhibit Na & Cl reabsorption → ↑ Na & Cl excretion → diuresis.
  3. ↓ Ca²⁺ excretion (paradoxical):
    • ↓ Na entry into DCT cell → ↓ intracellular Na → ↑ Na-Ca exchange on basolateral membrane → ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (paracellular).
    • Useful for idiopathic hypercalciuria & calcium oxalate kidney stones.
  4. ↑ K⁺ & H⁺ excretion:
    • ↑ Na delivery to collecting duct → ↑ Na reabsorption via ENaC → ↑ lumen-negative potential → ↑ K⁺ & H⁺ secretion (aldosterone effect).
    • Causes hypokalaemia & metabolic alkalosis.
  5. ↑ Mg²⁺ excretion — hypomagnesaemia (especially with loop diuretics).
  6. ↑ Uric acid reabsorption (competition with OAT) → hyperuricaemia; gout flare.
  7. Initial diuretic effect reduces blood volume → ↓ cardiac output; chronic effect — vasodilation (↓ vascular smooth muscle Na & Ca → ↓ contractility; ↓ vascular responsiveness to pressors); accounts for sustained BP lowering despite volume repletion.
  8. Anti-osteoporotic effect — ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption → ↑ bone mineral density; reduces hip fractures in elderly.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Oral; well absorbed; secreted into tubule via OAT (organic anion transporter) — must reach tubular lumen to act.
  • Half-life — HCTZ 6–12 h; chlorthalidone 24–72 h (longer; more potent); indapamide 14–18 h; metolazone 12–24 h.
  • Renal excretion; dose-adjust in CKD (less effective at GFR <30 — except metolazone which works at GFR >10).

Therapeutic Uses

  • Hypertension — first-line; especially elderly, isolated systolic HTN; low-dose HCTZ (12.5–25 mg) or chlorthalidone (12.5–25 mg); ALLHAT, SHEP, Syst-Eur trials.
  • Heart failure — for volume overload; combine with loop if resistant (sequential nephron blockade).
  • Oedema — mild-moderate; renal, hepatic, cardiac.
  • Osteoporosis — ↑ bone density; reduces hip fractures (observational).
  • Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — paradoxical antidiuretic effect (↓ plasma volume → ↓ GFR → ↑ proximal Na & water reabsorption → ↓ urine output).
  • Idiopathic hypercalciuria & calcium stones — ↓ urinary Ca²⁺.
  • Resistant hypertension — add to ACEI + CCB; chlorthalidone preferred (PATHWAY-2 — spironolactone superior to bisoprolol & doxazosin).

Adverse Effects

  • Electrolytes — hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia (mild).
  • Metabolic — hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia, ↑ triglycerides, ↑ LDL, ↑ total cholesterol (mild).
  • Volume depletion — hypotension, orthostatic.
  • Impotence, erectile dysfunction.
  • Photosensitivity, rash.
  • Hypersensitivity — sulfa allergy (cross-reactivity low <10%); Stevens-Johnson (rare).
  • Pancreatitis, cholecystitis (rare).

Clinical Pearl

Thiazides are first-line for hypertension — especially elderly, isolated systolic HTN; cheap; proven CV event reduction (ALLHAT, SHEP). Chlorthalidone preferred over HCTZ — longer half-life, more potent, more sustained BP reduction, more CV events reduction; but more hypokalaemia & hyponatraemia. Always check electrolytes (K, Na, Mg) & renal function 1–2 weeks after starting; supplement K or combine with K-sparing (amiloride, spironolactone). Thiazides ineffective at GFR <30 (except metolazone — works at GFR >10); combine with loop for sequential nephron blockade in resistant oedema. Use lowest effective dose (HCTZ 12.5–25 mg; chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg) — higher doses ↑ side effects without added BP benefit. India — thiazides underutilised despite being cheap & effective; HCTZ 12.5 mg widely available; chlorthalidone less common; combination with ACEI/ARB (FDC) improves adherence & BP control.

Introduction

Angina pectoris is the clinical syndrome of transient chest pain or discomfort due to myocardial ischaemia (imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand). Three main types — stable (chronic stable) angina, unstable angina, variant (Prinzmetal/vasospastic) angina. Treatment aims to restore the supply-demand balance — reduce demand (heart rate, contractility, wall stress) and/or increase supply (coronary vasodilation).

Classification of Drugs Used in Angina Pectoris (5 marks)

A. Organic Nitrates

  • Short-acting — Nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate, GTN) — sublingual tablet, spray; onset 1–3 min; duration 20–30 min.
  • Long-acting:
    • Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN) — sublingual, oral; duration 4–6 h.
    • Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN) — oral; duration 6–8 h.
    • Nitroglycerin transdermal patch, ointment — duration 8–14 h.
    • Erythrityl tetranitrate, pentaerythritol tetranitrate (rarely used).
    • Amyl nitrite (inhalant — historically for cyanide poisoning).

B. β-Adrenergic Blockers (β-Blockers)

  • Cardioselective (β1-selective) — Atenolol, Metoprolol, Bisoprolol, Nebivolol (also NO-mediated vasodilation), Acebutolol, Betaxolol, Esmolol (ultra-short-acting — IV).
  • Non-selective (β1 + β2) — Propranolol, Timolol, Nadolol, Sotalol (also class III antiarrhythmic).
  • Non-selective with α1-blockade — Carvedilol, Labetalol.

C. Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs)

  • Dihydropyridines (DHP) — predominantly vasodilators:
    • Short-acting — Nifedipine (avoid short-acting capsule — reflex tachycardia, hypotension).
    • Long-acting — Amlodipine, Felodipine, Nicardipine, Lercanidipine, Nitrendipine, Clevidipine (IV).
  • Non-dihydropyridines (Non-DHP) — predominantly cardiac depressants:
    • Phenylalkylamine — Verapamil.
    • Benzothiazepine — Diltiazem.

D. Antiplatelet & Antithrombotic Drugs

  • Aspirin — COX-1 inhibitor; ↓platelet aggregation.
  • Clopidogrel, Prasugrel, Ticagrelor — P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonists.
  • Heparin, LMWH (enoxaparin), Fondaparinux — anticoagulants (acute coronary syndromes).
  • Abciximab, Eptifibatide, Tirofiban — GP IIb/IIIa antagonists (PCI).
  • Rivaroxaban, Apixaban — factor Xa inhibitors (recent ACS trials).

E. Lipid-Lowering Drugs

  • Statins — Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin, Simvastatin, Pravastatin; HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors; plaque stabilisation; anti-inflammatory.
  • Ezetimibe — cholesterol absorption inhibitor.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors — Evolocumab, Alirocumab (familial hypercholesterolaemia, statin intolerance).
  • Bempedoic acid — ATP citrate lyase inhibitor.
  • Fibrates, Niacin, Omega-3 fatty acids — adjuncts.

F. Other Antianginal Drugs

  • Ranolazine — inhibits late sodium current (late INa) → ↓ Ca²⁺ overload → ↓ myocardial wall stress & oxygen demand; does not affect HR or BP; used for chronic stable angina refractory to standard therapy.
  • Ivabradine — selective inhibitor of If (funny channel) in SA node → ↓ heart rate without affecting contractility or BP; used for chronic stable angina in sinus rhythm with HR >70 bpm.
  • Nicorandil — nitrate + K-ATP channel opener; dual mechanism; vasodilator; used for stable angina.
  • Trimetazidine — inhibits fatty acid oxidation (3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase) → shifts to glucose oxidation → ↓ oxygen demand; metabolic modulator.
  • Molsidomine — NO donor (like nitrates).
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — reduce CV events; protect endothelium; especially in diabetes, LV dysfunction, hypertension.

G. Combination Therapy

  • β-blocker + DHP-CCB (amlodipine) — synergistic; β-blocker counters reflex tachycardia from DHP.
  • β-blocker + long-acting nitrate.
  • Nitrate + CCB (avoid non-DHP + β-blocker — bradycardia, AV block).
  • Antiplatelet + statin + ACEI — for secondary prevention.

Mechanism of Action of Nitrates (5 marks)

1. Pharmacokinetics

  • Nitroglycerin (GTN):
    • Sublingual — onset 1–3 min; peak 4–8 min; duration 20–30 min; bioavailability <5% oral (extensive first-pass); sublingual bypasses liver.
    • IV — for unstable angina, acute MI, acute heart failure, hypertensive emergency; titratable.
    • Transdermal patch, ointment — sustained release; 8–14 h duration; patch-off period (12 h) to prevent tolerance.
    • Metabolism — by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 (ALDH2) in liver, blood vessel walls; inactive metabolites (glyceryl dinitrate, mononitrate, glycerol).
  • Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN):
    • Sublingual — onset 2–5 min; duration 1–2 h.
    • Oral — onset 20–40 min; duration 4–6 h.
    • Hepatic metabolism to active ISMN (5-ISMN & 2-ISMN).
  • Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN):
    • Oral — 100% bioavailability (no first-pass); duration 6–8 h.
    • Slow-release formulation — once daily; patch-off period (≥8 h) to prevent tolerance.

2. Mechanism of Action

  1. Prodrug activation:
    • Organic nitrates are prodrugs; require enzymatic bioactivation to release nitric oxide (NO).
    • ALDH2 (mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2) — main enzyme for nitroglycerin; converts GTN to 1,2-glyceryl dinitrate + nitrite → NO.
    • Other enzymes — cytochrome P450 reductase, xanthine oxidoreductase, glutathione-S-transferase.
    • Released NO is identical to endogenous endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF) — discovered by Furchgott, Ignarro, Murad (Nobel Prize 1998).
  2. NO-mediated vasodilation:
    1. NO diffuses from endothelial cell (or from nitrate metabolism in vascular smooth muscle) to adjacent vascular smooth muscle cell.
    2. NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) → converts GTP → cyclic GMP (cGMP).
    3. cGMP activates protein kinase G (PKG).
    4. PKG phosphorylates multiple targets:

    5. ↓ Intracellular Ca²⁺ → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation.
  3. Vascular selectivity:
    • Low doses — preferential venodilation (capacitance veins) → ↓ venous return (preload) → ↓ ventricular end-diastolic volume & wall stress → ↓ myocardial oxygen demand.
    • Higher doses — arteriolar dilation (resistance arteries) → ↓ peripheral resistance → ↓ afterload → ↓ myocardial work.
    • Coronary arteries:
      • Dilates large epicardial coronary arteries (conductance vessels) — improves blood flow to ischaemic subendocardium; redistributes flow.
      • Dilates collateral coronary vessels → improves perfusion of ischaemic areas.

      • Little effect on arterioles (<100 µm) — prevents "coronary steal" syndrome.
    • Platelets — NO + cGMP → ↓ platelet aggregation; may reduce thrombosis in unstable angina.

3. Haemodynamic Effects

  • Venodilation → ↓ preload (ventricular end-diastolic pressure & volume) → ↓ myocardial wall stress → ↓ oxygen demand.
  • Arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload (systemic vascular resistance) → ↓ cardiac work → ↓ oxygen demand.
  • Coronary dilation → ↑ coronary blood flow; relief of spasm; redistribution to ischaemic subendocardium.
  • Reflex tachycardia — ↓ BP triggers baroreceptor reflex → ↑ sympathetic outflow → ↑ HR & contractility → may offset oxygen-sparing effect (combine with β-blocker).
  • Pulmonary vasodilation — ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance; useful in pulmonary oedema.
  • Reduced platelet aggregation — anti-thrombotic effect.

4. Therapeutic Uses

  • Acute anginal attack — sublingual GTN (1 tablet or spray under tongue; repeat every 5 min × 3 doses; if no relief, call emergency — possible MI).
  • Prophylaxis of stable angina — long-acting nitrates (ISMN, GTN patch) with patch-off period to prevent tolerance; β-blocker; CCB; aspirin; statin.
  • Variant (Prinzmetal) angina — nitrates + CCBs (especially DHP); avoid β-blockers (may worsen spasm via unopposed α).
  • Unstable angina / NSTEMI — IV nitroglycerin; antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor); anticoagulant (heparin/LMWH); statin; β-blocker; coronary angiography ± PCI.
  • Acute MI — IV nitroglycerin (if BP allows); aspirin; clopidogrel; heparin; β-blocker; ACEI; statin; primary PCI or thrombolysis.
  • Acute left ventricular failure / pulmonary oedema — IV/sublingual GTN; venodilation reduces preload; afterload reduction improves cardiac output.
  • Hypertensive emergency — IV nitroprusside (arterial + venous vasodilation); IV nitroglycerin (especially if cardiac ischaemia).
  • Chronic heart failure — ISDN + hydralazine (especially in African-Americans — A-HeFT trial with fixed-dose Bidil).
  • Anal fissure — topical GTN 0.2–0.4% ointment (relieves internal anal sphincter spasm).
  • Cyanide poisoning — sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate; amyl nitrite (forms methaemoglobin which binds cyanide).
  • Esophageal spasm, biliary colic — sublingual GTN may relieve smooth muscle spasm.

5. Adverse Effects

  • Vasodilatory:
    • Headache (most common; ~50%) — meningeal vasodilation; ameliorates with continued use; treat with paracetamol.
    • Flushing, dizziness, postural hypotension, syncope.
    • Reflex tachycardia — may worsen angina; combine with β-blocker.
  • Methaemoglobinaemia — high doses or prolonged use; nitrites oxidise Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ in haemoglobin; ↓ oxygen-carrying capacity; treat with methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV.
  • Tolerance (nitrate tolerance) — develops with continuous therapy (>24 h); due to:
    • Depletion of sulphydryl (-SH) groups (required for ALDH2-mediated NO release) — "thiol hypothesis".
    • ↑ ALDH2 inactivation by oxidative stress.
    • ↑ Superoxide production → ↑ NO degradation (uncoupling of eNOS).
    • Neurohormonal activation — RAAS, sympathetic activation.
    • Plasma volume expansion.
  • Prevention — nitrate-free interval (≥8–12 h daily); eccentric dosing (e.g., ISMN at 8 AM & 2 PM — nitrate-free overnight); intermittent transdermal patch (12 h on, 12 h off).
  • Withdrawal / rebound — abrupt cessation of long-term nitrate therapy → rebound vasoconstriction, angina, MI; taper gradually.
  • Alcohol interaction — severe hypotension; avoid concurrent use.
  • Sildenafil (PDE5 inhibitor) interaction — contraindicated; both ↑ cGMP → severe, life-threatening hypotension; at least 24 h gap (48 h for tadalafil).
  • Increased intracranial pressure — vasodilation; avoid in raised ICP, recent head injury.
  • Increased intraocular pressure — historical concern (open-angle glaucoma); modern evidence suggests safe.
  • Contact dermatitis — transdermal patch.
  • Sodium nitroprusside — cyanide & thiocyanate toxicity (with prolonged use >48 h or renal impairment); monitor thiocyanate levels; treat with sodium thiosulfate + hydroxocobalamin.

6. Contraindications

  • Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg).
  • Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) — ↓ preload worsens outflow obstruction.
  • Right ventricular infarction — ↓ preload worsens RV failure.
  • Recent PDE5 inhibitor use (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) — within 24–48 h.
  • Severe anaemia (methaemoglobinaemia risk).
  • Raised intracranial pressure (head injury, haemorrhage).
  • Hypersensitivity to nitrates.
  • Constrictive pericarditis, cardiac tamponade.

Introduction

Digoxin — a cardiac glycoside from Digitalis lanata; inhibits Na-K-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na → ↓ Na-Ca exchange → ↑ intracellular Ca → ↑ contractility (positive inotropy); also ↑ vagal tone → ↓ AV conduction (rate control in AF). Narrow therapeutic index (0.5–0.9 ng/mL); toxicity common.

Predisposing Factors

  • Hypokalaemia — most important; K⁺ competes with digoxin for Na-K-ATPase; low K⁺ → ↑ digoxin binding → ↑ toxicity.
  • Hypomagnesaemia — similar mechanism; common with diuretics.
  • Hypercalcaemia — ↑ digoxin effect; additive with Ca²⁺.
  • Renal impairment — digoxin excreted unchanged by kidneys; ↑ levels in CKD; dose-adjust.
  • Advanced age — ↓ renal function, ↓ lean body mass.
  • Hypothyroidism — ↓ renal clearance, ↑ digoxin sensitivity.
  • Cardiac disease — acute MI, myocarditis, severe HF, amyloidosis (↑ sensitivity to digoxin).
  • Drug interactions:
    • ↑ Digoxin levels — verapamil, diltiazem, amiodarone, quinidine, propafenone, flecainide, clarithromycin, erythromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, dronedarone, ranolazine, alprazolam, spironolactone (also raises digoxin levels via P-gp inhibition; also metabolite cross-reactivity in some assays), tiagabine, carvedilol, PPIs (mild), atorvastatin (high dose).
    • Additive bradycardia — β-blockers, non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem), ivabradine.
    • Additive AV block — β-blockers, non-DHP CCBs, amiodarone.
    • Hypokalaemia — loop & thiazide diuretics, corticosteroids, amphotericin B, cisplatin, β2-agonists.
  • Electrolyte depletion — diarrhoea, vomiting, dialysis.
  • Acid-base disturbances — alkalosis (↓ K⁺); acidosis (↑ digoxin dissociation).
  • Reduced lean body mass — elderly, malnutrition; ↓ distribution volume.

Clinical Manifestations

1. Cardiac (Most Important & Dangerous)

  • Almost any arrhythmia can occur — due to ↑ automaticity (Ca²⁺ overload → delayed afterdepolarisations) + ↑ vagal tone (AV block).
  • Classic — atrial tachycardia with AV block (PAT with block); bidirectional VT (alternating QRS axis — pathognomonic); premature ventricular contractions (PVCs — bigeminy, multiform); ventricular tachycardia; ventricular fibrillation; atrial fibrillation (paradoxical — regularised AF with complete heart block & junctional escape); sinus bradycardia; AV block (1st, 2nd, 3rd degree).
  • ECG findings — ST segment depression ("sagging" or "scooped" — reverse check mark); T wave inversion or peaking; short QT; U waves; prolonged PR (AV block).
  • Note — ST changes are common at therapeutic doses; do NOT indicate toxicity.

2. Gastrointestinal (Often Earliest)

  • Anorexia (often first symptom); nausea, vomiting; abdominal pain; diarrhoea.

3. Neurological

  • Headache, fatigue, malaise, drowsiness, confusion, weakness.
  • Visual disturbances — pathognomonic:
    • Blurred vision, photophobia.
    • Chromatopsia — objects appear yellow or green (xanthopsia); less commonly red, blue, brown.
    • Halos around lights (coloured — yellow, green, white).
    • Scotomas, tunnel vision, amblyopia.
  • Delirium, hallucinations, psychosis — especially elderly.
  • Neuralgia, paraesthesia.
  • Seizures (rare).

4. Other

  • Gynaecomastia (digoxin has oestrogen-like structure).
  • Skin rash, urticaria.
  • Thrombocytopenia (rare).
  • Eosinophilia (hypersensitivity).

Diagnosis

  • Clinical suspicion — symptoms + risk factors + ECG.
  • Serum digoxin level:
    • Therapeutic range — 0.5–0.9 ng/mL (heart failure); 0.8–2 ng/mL (AF rate control; modern lower targets preferred).
    • Toxicity usually >2 ng/mL; but can occur at "therapeutic" levels if hypokalaemic, hypomagnesaemic, hypercalcaemic, or in renal failure/elderly.
    • Draw at least 6 h after last dose (distribution phase complete).
    • False elevation — endogenous digoxin-like immunoreactive substances (DLIS) in renal failure, liver disease, pregnancy, neonates.
    • Spironolactone & its metabolites cross-react with some digoxin immunoassays — falsely elevated levels.
  • Serum potassium — hypokalaemia predisposes & worsens toxicity; hyperkalaemia indicates acute massive overdose (Na-K-ATPase inhibition → K⁺ leaks out of cells).
  • Magnesium, calcium, renal function, LFT.
  • ECG — arrhythmias, ST changes (note — ST changes alone don't indicate toxicity).
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring.

Management

1. Stop Digoxin & Offending Drugs

  • Stop digoxin; stop interacting drugs (diuretics if causing hypokalaemia; verapamil, amiodarone).
  • Identify & correct precipitant — hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, dehydration, renal failure.

2. Correct Electrolytes

  • Hypokalaemia — correct aggressively; IV KCl 10–20 mEq/h (max 20 mEq/h peripheral, 40 mEq/h central); target K⁺ 4.0–5.0 mEq/L; caution in AV block (K⁺ also slows AV conduction).
  • Hypomagnesaemia — IV magnesium sulphate 1–2 g (over 10–20 min); correct even if serum Mg normal (intracellular depletion).
  • Hyperkalaemia (acute overdose) — insulin + dextrose; calcium (controversial — theoretical risk of "stone heart" with digoxin + Ca²⁺, but recent data shows safe); avoid β2-agonists if possible (hypokalaemia); dialysis ineffective (digoxin has large Vd).

3. Treat Arrhythmias

  • Supraventricular arrhythmias (atrial tachycardia with block, AF) — usually respond to digoxin Fab antibody; avoid class Ia (quinidine, procainamide — worsen toxicity); avoid verapamil, β-blockers (worsen AV block); consider amiodarone if Fab unavailable.
  • Ventricular arrhythmias (VT, VF, PVCs) — lidocaine (class Ib — safest in digoxin toxicity); phenytoin (also class Ib — historically used); magnesium sulphate (suppresses afterdepolarisations); avoid class Ia (quinidine, procainamide — ↑ digoxin levels & toxicity); electrical cardioversion — last resort (risk of VT/VF — use lowest energy, synchronised if possible).
  • Bradycardia & AV block — atropine 0.5–1 mg IV (may be ineffective); transcutaneous or transvenous pacing; isoproterenol (avoid if myocardial ischaemia); Fab antibody.
  • Bidirectional VT — Fab antibody + lidocaine + magnesium.

4. Activated Charcoal

  • For acute oral overdose within 1–2 h; multiple doses may interrupt enterohepatic circulation.

5. Digoxin-Specific Antibody (Fab) — DigiFab / Digibind

  • Indications:
    • Life-threatening arrhythmia (VT, VF, complete heart block, severe bradycardia).
    • Hyperkalaemia (>5.5 mEq/L) in acute overdose.
    • Cardiac arrest due to digoxin.
    • Hypotension, shock.
    • Serum digoxin >10 ng/mL (acute) or >6 ng/mL (chronic).
    • Acute ingestion >10 mg (adults) or >4 mg (children).
    • End-organ dysfunction (severe altered mental status, visual changes).
  • Dose calculation:
    • Empirical — 1–2 vials (40 mg/vial) if chronic toxicity with life-threatening features; 3–6 vials for acute overdose.
    • Based on serum digoxin: Dose (vials) = [Serum digoxin (ng/mL) × Weight (kg)] / 100.
    • Based on ingested dose: Dose (vials) = Ingested dose (mg) / 0.5 (each vial binds 0.5 mg digoxin).
    • Round up; give half bolus, then infusion if needed.
  • Mechanism — ovine monoclonal antibody fragments (Fab); bind free digoxin in plasma → form inactive complex → renal excretion; shifts digoxin from tissues to plasma.
  • Effect — within 30–45 min; reverses arrhythmias, hyperkalaemia, symptoms.
  • Adverse effects:
    • Hypokalaemia (digoxin inhibition removed → K⁺ re-enters cells) — monitor & replace.
    • Worsening of underlying heart failure (loss of digoxin inotropic effect).
    • Atrial fibrillation (loss of rate control).
    • Allergic reactions (rash, anaphylaxis — low risk; ovine protein).
    • Rebound toxicity — if large tissue digoxin stores redistribute; monitor 24 h.
    • Serum digoxin level rises dramatically after Fab (bound + free) — do NOT recheck levels for days (misleading).
  • Cost — expensive; reserve for severe cases.

6. Haemodialysis

  • Ineffective — digoxin has large Vd (~500 L); tissue-bound; not removed by dialysis.
  • May be needed for hyperkalaemia or renal failure.

Prevention

  • Maintain serum digoxin 0.5–0.9 ng/mL (heart failure); 0.8–2 ng/mL (AF).
  • Maintain K⁺ >4.0, Mg²⁺ >2.0 mEq/L.
  • Dose-adjust for renal function (CrCl); reduce dose in elderly.
  • Avoid unnecessary drug interactions; check before adding new drugs.
  • Monitor ECG, K⁺, Mg²⁺, renal function.
  • Patient education — recognise early symptoms (anorexia, nausea, visual changes); avoid excessive potassium loss (diuretics, diarrhoea); dietary salt substitutes (contain KCl — beneficial).
  • Use lower doses in elderly, CKD, low body weight.
  • Avoid in Brugada syndrome, WPW with AF (can accelerate accessory pathway), HOCM (outflow obstruction).

Clinical Pearl

Digoxin toxicity should be suspected in any patient on digoxin with new GI symptoms, visual changes (yellow halos, xanthopsia), confusion, or arrhythmias. Classic arrhythmia — atrial tachycardia with AV block (PAT with block); bidirectional VT is pathognomonic. Hypokalaemia is the most important precipitant — K⁺ competes with digoxin for Na-K-ATPase; always check K⁺; correct aggressively (IV KCl); also check Mg²⁺ (correct even if normal). Digoxin-specific Fab antibody (DigiFab) is the antidote — binds free digoxin → inactive complex → renal excretion; indications — life-threatening arrhythmia, hyperkalaemia >5.5 in acute overdose, serum digoxin >10 ng/mL; effect within 30–45 min. After Fab, serum digoxin level rises dramatically (bound + free measured) — do NOT recheck levels for 3–4 days (misleading); monitor clinically & ECG. Watch for hypokalaemia after Fab — digoxin inhibition removed → K⁺ re-enters cells; replace aggressively. Avoid class Ia antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide — worsen toxicity); use lidocaine or phenytoin (class Ib — safest for ventricular arrhythmias); magnesium sulphate for afterdepolarisation suppression. Avoid calcium in acute overdose with hyperkalaemia — theoretical "stone heart" (controversial — recent data shows safe); use insulin + dextrose for hyperkalaemia. Always dose-adjust for renal function — digoxin excreted unchanged by kidneys; reduce dose in CKD & elderly. Drug interactions — verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine, clarithromycin, itraconazole, cyclosporine, dronedarone ↑ digoxin levels (P-gp inhibition); always check before adding new drugs. India — digoxin still widely used (cheap; AF rate control in heart failure); toxicity common due to inadequate monitoring; physician & patient education about K⁺ & renal function critical; DigiFab expensive & limited availability.
